tracks.name: Linux Fundamentals
tracks.description: Master the core text-processing tools every Linux user needs.

lessons.title: grep: Search Like a Pro
lessons.introduction: grep (Global Regular Expression Print) is one of the most powerful text search tools in Linux. It searches for patterns in files and streams, making it indispensable for log analysis, code review, and data extraction.
lessons.purpose: Search for patterns in text files and streams

sections.title: Basic Search
sections.content: The simplest use of grep is searching for a literal string in a file.
sections.example: grep 'ERROR' server.log
sections.explanation: Prints every line in server.log that contains the word ERROR

sections.title: Case-Insensitive Search
sections.content: Use -i to ignore case differences.
sections.example: grep -i 'error' server.log
sections.explanation: Matches ERROR, error, Error, eRrOr — all of them

sections.title: Show Line Numbers
sections.content: Use -n to display line numbers of matches.
sections.example: grep -n 'CRITICAL' server.log
sections.explanation: Shows exactly where critical events occur in your log

sections.title: Count Matches
sections.content: Use -c to count matching lines instead of printing them.
sections.example: grep -c 'ERROR' server.log
sections.explanation: Returns a single count — great for quick health checks

sections.title: Invert Match
sections.content: Use -v to show lines that do NOT match.
sections.example: grep -v '#' server.log
sections.explanation: Strips comment lines from config files or logs

sections.title: Extended Regex
sections.content: Use -E to enable | (OR), + and ? quantifiers.
sections.example: grep -E 'ERROR|WARN|CRITICAL' server.log
sections.explanation: Matches any of the three severity levels in one pass

sections.title: Context Lines
sections.content: Use -A, -B, -C to show surrounding context lines.
sections.example: grep -C 3 'FATAL' server.log
sections.explanation: Shows 3 lines before and after each FATAL — vital for debugging

sections.title: Extract Only Match
sections.content: Use -o to print only the matched portion, not the whole line.
sections.explanation: Extracts just the IP addresses — nothing else

common_mistakes: Forgetting -E for extended regex (| and + won't work without it)
Using grep on binary files — use grep -a to treat as text
Case sensitivity — always consider -i if unsure
best_practices: Chain grep calls: grep 'ERROR' log | grep -v 'test' to narrow results
Use --color=auto for readable highlighted output
Combine -l (list files) with -r for codebase-wide searches

exercises.prompt: Count how many ERROR lines are in server.log
exercises.hint: Use -c flag

exercises.prompt: Show all lines NOT containing 'INFO' in server.log
exercises.hint: Invert with -v

exercises.prompt: Extract only IP addresses from apache.log
exercises.hint: Use -oE with an IP regex pattern

quiz.question: Which grep flag makes the search case-insensitive?
quiz.explanation: -i stands for ignore-case. -c counts, -v inverts, -n shows line numbers.

quiz.question: How do you count matching lines with grep?
quiz.explanation: -c (count) returns only the number of matching lines.

quiz.question: To search for 'error' OR 'warning' in a file, you need flag ___
quiz.explanation: -E enables extended regular expressions which support the | alternation operator.

lessons.title: sed: Stream Editing Mastery
lessons.introduction: sed (Stream EDitor) processes text line by line, applying editing commands. It's perfect for find-and-replace, deletion, insertion, and complex text transformations — without opening a text editor.
lessons.purpose: Edit text streams non-interactively — substitute, delete, insert

sections.title: Basic Substitution
sections.content: The s command substitutes text: s/OLD/NEW/ replaces first match per line, s/OLD/NEW/g replaces all.
sections.example: sed 's/ERROR/ALERT/g' server.log
sections.explanation: Replaces every occurrence of ERROR with ALERT in every line

sections.title: Delete Lines
sections.content: The d command deletes lines matching a pattern.
sections.example: sed '/^#/d' server.log
sections.explanation: Removes all comment lines (starting with #)

sections.title: Print Specific Lines
sections.content: Use -n with p to print only specified lines.
sections.example: sed -n '10,20p' server.log
sections.explanation: Prints only lines 10 through 20 — like a precise head/tail

sections.title: In-Place Editing
sections.content: Use -i to edit files in-place (WARNING: destructive!).
sections.example: sed -i 's/localhost/127.0.0.1/g' config.txt
sections.explanation: Modifies the actual file. Use -i.bak to keep a backup.

sections.title: Address Ranges
sections.content: Apply commands only to lines matching a range or pattern.
sections.example: sed '/START/,/END/d' file.txt
sections.explanation: Deletes everything between START and END markers

sections.title: Multiple Commands
sections.content: Chain multiple sed commands with -e or semicolons.
sections.example: sed -e 's/foo/bar/g' -e '/^$/d' file.txt
sections.explanation: Replace foo with bar AND remove blank lines in one pass

common_mistakes: Forgetting /g flag — without it, only the first match per line is replaced
Using -i without a backup on important files
Special characters in patterns need escaping: . * [ \ ^ $ need \
best_practices: Test without -i first, add it only when output looks correct
Use single quotes around sed expressions to prevent shell interpretation
Combine with grep -n first to find line numbers before editing

exercises.prompt: Replace all commas with pipes in employees.csv (print to stdout)
exercises.hint: Use s/,/|/g

exercises.prompt: Remove all blank lines from server.log
exercises.hint: The pattern ^$ matches empty lines

quiz.question: What does sed 's/a/b/' do without the /g flag?
options: Replaces only the first 'a' per line
quiz.answer: Replaces only the first 'a' per line
quiz.explanation: Without /g (global), sed only replaces the first match on each line.

lessons.title: awk: Data Extraction Engine
lessons.introduction: awk is a complete programming language built for text processing. It reads input line by line, splits each line into fields, and lets you write programs that process, filter, and compute on structured text data.
lessons.purpose: Field-based text processing, filtering, arithmetic, and report generation

sections.title: Field Access
sections.content: awk splits each line by whitespace. $1 is field 1, $2 is field 2, $0 is the whole line, NF is number of fields.
sections.example: awk '{print $1}' apache.log
sections.explanation: Prints the first field (IP address) from every line

sections.title: Custom Delimiter
sections.content: Use -F to set the field separator.
sections.example: awk -F',' '{print $2,$4}' employees.csv
sections.explanation: Treats CSV commas as separators, prints name and salary

sections.title: Pattern Filtering
sections.content: awk programs have the form: PATTERN { ACTION }. Only run action on matching lines.
sections.example: awk '/ERROR/ {print $0}' server.log
sections.explanation: Same as grep ERROR but with awk's processing power available

sections.title: Arithmetic
sections.content: awk can do math. Sum a column, compute averages, compare values.
sections.example: awk -F',' 'NR>1 {sum+=$4} END {print sum/NR}' employees.csv
sections.explanation: Computes average salary (skipping header row)

sections.title: NR and FNR
sections.content: NR is the total record (line) number. FNR resets per file. Useful for skipping headers with NR>1.
sections.example: awk -F',' 'NR>1 {print $2}' employees.csv
sections.explanation: Skips the header line and prints only employee names

sections.title: Associative Arrays
sections.content: awk has hash maps built in — perfect for grouping and counting.
sections.example: awk '{count[$1]++} END {for(ip in count) print count[ip], ip}' apache.log
sections.explanation: Counts requests per IP address — no sort|uniq needed

common_mistakes: Forgetting NR>1 to skip CSV headers
Using == for string comparison (correct) vs = for assignment
Forgetting END block for final output after processing all lines
best_practices: Use printf for formatted output: printf "%-20s %5d\n", name, count
Initialize variables explicitly: BEGIN {sum=0}
Test with NR<=5 first to see output before processing the whole file

exercises.prompt: Print only the department column (col 3) from employees.csv, skipping the header
exercises.hint: Use -F',' and NR>1

exercises.prompt: Count how many requests each HTTP status code got in apache.log
exercises.solution: awk '{count[$9]++} END {for(s in count) print count[s], s}' apache.log | sort -rn
exercises.hint: Field 9 is the status code. Use an associative array.

quiz.question: In awk, what does $0 represent?
quiz.explanation: $0 is the entire record (line). $1 is field 1, $NF is the last field, NR is the line number.

quiz.question: To set comma as the field separator in awk, use flag ___
quiz.explanation: -F sets the field separator. -F',' makes awk treat commas as delimiters.

lessons.title: Advanced grep: Power Search Techniques
lessons.introduction: grep becomes exponentially more powerful with Perl-compatible regex, multiple pattern matching, binary file handling, and context control. These advanced features are essential for complex log analysis and data extraction.
lessons.purpose: Perform complex searches with Perl regex, multiple patterns, and context control

sections.title: Perl-Compatible Regex (PCRE)
sections.content: grep -P enables Perl-compatible regex with \d (digits), \w (word chars), \s (whitespace), non-greedy matching, and lookaround assertions.
sections.example: grep -P '\d{3}-\d{3}-\d{4}' server.log
sections.explanation: Extracts phone numbers in format 123-456-7890 using Perl regex digit matching

sections.title: Multiple Patterns with -e
sections.content: Use -e to specify multiple search patterns. grep matches lines containing ANY of the patterns.
sections.example: grep -e 'ERROR' -e 'FATAL' -e 'CRITICAL' server.log
sections.explanation: Searches for three different severity levels in a single pass

sections.title: Context Lines: -A, -B, -C
sections.content: Show lines After (-A), Before (-B), or both sides of context (-C) around each match.
sections.example: grep -A 2 -B 2 'ERROR' server.log
sections.explanation: Shows 2 lines before and after each ERROR for full debugging context

sections.title: Binary File Handling
sections.content: grep -a treats binary files as text. grep -I skips binary files entirely. Essential when scanning mixed file types.
sections.example: grep -r -I 'password' .
sections.explanation: Recursively searches for 'password' but skips binary files to avoid garbled output

sections.title: Pattern Files with -f
sections.content: Read patterns from a file, one per line. Perfect for matching many terms at once.
sections.example: grep -f patterns.txt server.log
sections.explanation: Each line in patterns.txt is a separate pattern to match — great for blocklists

sections.title: Advanced Extraction with -oP
sections.content: Combine -o (only match) with -P (Perl regex) for precise data extraction.
sections.example: grep -oP 'user=\K\w+' server.log
sections.explanation: Uses \K to reset the match start, extracting only the username after 'user='

common_mistakes: Using grep without -P when Perl regex features are needed — \d \w \s won't work with basic grep
Forgetting that grep -a treats binary files as text — can produce unexpected output
Using -e with patterns containing spaces — always quote the pattern
best_practices: Use grep -P when you need \d, \w, \s, or lookaround assertions
Combine -oP with \K for clean extraction of specific data fields
Use grep -rI for recursive searches that skip binary files

exercises.prompt: Extract all IP addresses from server.log using Perl regex, deduplicated
exercises.hint: Use grep -oP with a Perl regex for IP addresses

exercises.prompt: Find all lines in server.log containing ERROR with 3 lines of context before and after
exercises.hint: Use -C for context lines on both sides of the match

quiz.question: Which grep flag enables Perl-compatible regular expressions?
quiz.explanation: -P enables PCRE (Perl-Compatible Regular Expressions) which supports \d, \w, \s, and lookaround.

quiz.question: What does grep -o do differently from regular grep?
options: Only prints the matched portion, not the whole line
Outputs to a file instead of stdout
Only matches at the start of lines
quiz.answer: Only prints the matched portion, not the whole line
quiz.explanation: -o prints only the matched text, stripping the rest of the line. Essential for data extraction.

tracks.name: Text Processing Mastery
tracks.description: Master the classic Unix text-processing toolkit.

lessons.title: cut, sort & uniq: The Classic Trio
lessons.introduction: cut, sort, and uniq are three complementary tools that together handle most data wrangling tasks. cut extracts columns, sort orders lines, and uniq deduplicates — together they form the backbone of Unix data pipelines.
lessons.purpose: Extract columns, sort data, and remove duplicates

sections.title: cut: Column Extraction
sections.content: cut extracts portions of each line. Use -d for delimiter and -f for field numbers.
sections.example: cut -d',' -f2,4 employees.csv
sections.explanation: Extracts name (field 2) and salary (field 4) from the CSV

sections.title: cut Character Ranges
sections.content: Without -d, cut works on character positions with -c.
sections.example: cut -c1-15 server.log
sections.explanation: Extracts the first 15 characters — useful for fixed-width formats

sections.title: sort: Ordering Lines
sections.content: sort arranges lines alphabetically by default. -n for numeric, -r for reverse, -k for a specific field.
sections.example: sort -t',' -k4 -rn employees.csv
sections.explanation: Sorts CSV by salary column (4) in descending numeric order

sections.title: sort Unique
sections.content: sort -u both sorts and removes duplicates in one step.
sections.example: awk '{print $1}' apache.log | sort -u
sections.explanation: Gets unique IPs without needing to pipe through uniq

sections.title: uniq: Deduplication
sections.content: uniq removes adjacent duplicate lines. Always sort first! -c adds counts, -d shows only duplicates.
sections.example: sort server.log | uniq -c | sort -rn
sections.explanation: Counts and ranks the most repeated log messages

sections.title: The Power Pipeline
sections.content: Combining all three gives you instant data analytics.
sections.example: cut -d',' -f3 employees.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
sections.explanation: Instantly shows employee count per department, ranked

common_mistakes: Using uniq without sort first — it only removes adjacent duplicates
Forgetting -n with sort for numeric sorting (10 sorts before 9 alphabetically)
cut fields start at 1, not 0
best_practices: Prefer awk -F for CSV when fields might contain commas within quotes
sort -u is faster than sort | uniq for simple deduplication
Use -k2 -k1 with sort for secondary sort keys

exercises.prompt: List all unique departments in employees.csv (sorted alphabetically)
exercises.hint: Column 3, skip header, deduplicate

exercises.prompt: Show frequency count of each HTTP status code in apache.log, highest first
exercises.hint: Extract field 9, then sort|uniq -c|sort -rn

quiz.question: Why must you sort before using uniq?
options: uniq requires sorted input to function at all
quiz.explanation: uniq compares consecutive lines. Non-adjacent duplicates won't be caught unless the input is sorted first.

lessons.title: tr, wc, head & tail: The Utilities Belt
lessons.introduction: Four small but essential tools: tr translates characters, wc counts things, head shows the start, tail shows the end. They appear in almost every serious pipeline.
lessons.purpose: Character translation, counting, and file slicing
lessons.syntax: tr SET1 SET2  |  wc [-l|-w|-c]  |  head/tail [-n N]

sections.title: wc: Word Count
sections.content: wc counts lines (-l), words (-w), or bytes (-c).
sections.example: wc -l server.log
sections.explanation: How many log entries? wc -l tells you instantly

sections.title: head: Top of File
sections.content: head shows the first N lines (default 10).
sections.example: head -20 server.log
sections.explanation: Preview a log file without loading the whole thing

sections.title: tail: End of File
sections.content: tail shows the last N lines. tail -f follows new lines as they're appended (live log monitoring).
sections.example: tail -100 server.log
sections.explanation: See the most recent 100 log entries

sections.title: tail -n +N: Skip Lines
sections.content: tail -n +2 skips the first line — the standard way to strip CSV headers.
sections.example: tail -n +2 employees.csv | wc -l
sections.explanation: Counts data rows excluding the header

sections.title: tr: Character Translation
sections.content: tr translates or deletes characters. Use it to change case, replace chars, or squeeze spaces.
sections.example: echo 'hello world' | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'
sections.explanation: Converts lowercase to uppercase

sections.title: tr for Tokenization
sections.content: tr -s '[:space:]' '\n' splits any whitespace-separated text into one word per line.
sections.example: cat server.log | tr -s '[:space:]' '\n' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10
sections.explanation: Word frequency analysis of a log file in one pipeline

common_mistakes: tail -f vs tail -n — -f follows, -n picks line count
wc -l counts newlines, so a file with no trailing newline shows one less
tr works on characters, not strings — use sed for multi-char replacement
best_practices: Use head -c 1M to preview the first megabyte of a large file
Combine: tail -n +2 file | head -100 to get lines 2–101
tr -d '\r' fixes Windows line endings (CRLF → LF)

exercises.prompt: Count the exact number of data rows in employees.csv (excluding header)
exercises.hint: Skip first line with tail -n +2, then count

exercises.prompt: Convert all text in server.log to uppercase
exercises.hint: tr can translate character ranges

quiz.question: What does tail -n +2 do?
options: Skips the first line and shows rest
Shows lines starting from line 2 onwards
quiz.answer: Skips the first line and shows rest
quiz.explanation: -n +2 means 'start from line 2' — effectively skipping line 1. Used to strip headers.

lessons.title: paste, column & friends: Column Masters
lessons.introduction: paste, column, expand, unexpand, and fold are lightweight tools for reshaping text into columns and rows. They transform messy or misaligned text into clean, human-readable output — no complex scripts needed.
lessons.purpose: Format text into aligned columns, merge files side-by-side, and reshape text

sections.title: paste: Merge Files by Lines
sections.content: paste combines corresponding lines from multiple files. -d sets the delimiter. -s transposes (merges all lines of each file into one line).
sections.example: paste -d',' names.txt salaries.txt > combined.csv
sections.explanation: Merges two files side-by-side with comma delimiter — instant CSV creation

sections.title: paste -s: Transpose and Sum
sections.content: paste -s merges all lines of a file into one line. Combined with -d and bc, it's great for arithmetic.
sections.example: paste -sd'+' numbers.txt | bc
sections.explanation: Joins all numbers with + and pipes to bc for sum calculation

sections.title: column -t: Auto-Align Tables
sections.content: column -t auto-formats text into aligned columns. -s sets the input delimiter. Essential for readable output.
sections.example: awk -F',' '{print $2, $3, $4}' employees.csv | column -t
sections.explanation: Takes space-separated awk output and aligns it into neat columns

sections.title: column with Delimiter
sections.content: Use -s to specify the input delimiter and -t for table formatting. Works with any separator.
sections.example: cat /etc/passwd | column -s: -t
sections.explanation: Formats the colon-delimited passwd file into aligned columns

sections.title: expand: Tabs to Spaces
sections.content: expand converts tab characters to spaces. -t N sets tab stops every N columns. Essential for normalizing whitespace.
sections.example: expand -t 8 file.txt | column -t
sections.explanation: First normalizes tabs to spaces, then aligns into columns

sections.title: fold: Line Wrapping
sections.content: fold wraps long lines at a specified width. -s breaks at spaces (word boundaries). -w sets the width.
sections.example: fold -s -w 80 server.log | head -50
sections.explanation: Wraps long log lines at 80 columns, breaking at word boundaries for readability

common_mistakes: Using paste without -d — defaults to tab separator which may not be what you want
Forgetting that column -t needs consistent delimiters — mixed whitespace breaks alignment
Using fold without -s — it breaks mid-word, making output hard to read
best_practices: Use paste -sd'+' numbers.txt | bc for quick sums of numeric files
Pipe any command's output through column -t for instant table formatting
Use expand before column when input contains tabs

exercises.prompt: Merge employees.csv columns 2 (name) and 3 (department) into a formatted table
exercises.hint: Use awk to extract columns, pipe to column -t for alignment

exercises.prompt: Convert all tabs in server.log to 4-space columns and show the first 20 lines
exercises.hint: Use expand -t 4 to convert tabs to spaces

quiz.question: What does paste -s do?
options: Pastes files side by side line by line
Merges all lines of each file into a single line
Stops paste after the first file
quiz.answer: Merges all lines of each file into a single line
quiz.explanation: -s (serial) merges all lines of each input file into one line, useful for creating delimited strings.

quiz.question: To convert tab characters to spaces, use command ___
quiz.explanation: expand converts tabs to spaces with configurable tab stops (-t N). unexpand does the reverse.

tracks.name: Regex Academy
tracks.description: Master regular expressions — the Swiss Army knife of text patterns.

lessons.title: Regular Expressions: Pattern Mastery
lessons.introduction: Regular expressions are a pattern language for describing text. They power grep, sed, awk, and virtually every programming language. Learning regex is one of the highest-leverage skills in computing — a few hours of study saves thousands of hours of manual text work.
lessons.purpose: Match, extract, and transform text using declarative patterns

sections.title: Anchors: ^ and $
sections.content: ^ matches the start of a line, $ matches the end. Anchors let you be precise about where a pattern must appear.
sections.example: grep '^ERROR' server.log
sections.explanation: Matches only lines that START with ERROR (not 'caught ERROR')

sections.title: Any Character: Dot
sections.content: The . (dot) matches any single character except newline.
sections.example: grep 'ERR.R' server.log
sections.explanation: Matches ERROR, ERR0R, ERR_R — anything in position 4

sections.title: Quantifiers: * + ?
sections.content: * means zero or more, + means one or more, ? means zero or one. Apply to the preceding element.
sections.example: grep -E 'ERR+OR' server.log
sections.explanation: ERR+OR matches ERRRROR — one or more R's between E and OR

sections.title: Character Classes: []
sections.content: [abc] matches any one of a, b, or c. [a-z] matches any lowercase letter. [^abc] matches anything NOT in the set.
sections.explanation: Matches IP-like patterns: three digits, dot, three digits

sections.title: Alternation: |
sections.content: The | operator means OR. It matches either the left or right expression. Requires -E in grep.
sections.example: grep -E 'ERROR|WARN|CRIT' server.log
sections.explanation: Matches any of three severity levels

sections.title: Grouping: ()
sections.content: Parentheses group expressions and capture for backreferences in sed.
sections.example: sed -E 's/(ERROR): (.*)/[\1] \2/' server.log
sections.explanation: Captures ERROR and the message, rearranges the format

sections.title: Escape Sequences
sections.content: \d matches digits, \w matches word chars, \s matches whitespace — in grep -P (Perl) or awk.
sections.explanation: Extracts IPv4 addresses using Perl-compatible regex

common_mistakes: Forgetting -E for | and + — basic grep doesn't support them
Dot matches everything including literal dot — escape it: \.
Greedy matching: .* grabs as much as possible — use .*? for lazy in Perl regex
best_practices: Build patterns incrementally and test with a small file first
Use grep -P for Perl regex (\d, \w, \s) when available
Online testers like regex101.com help visualize what your pattern matches

exercises.prompt: Extract all IPv4 addresses from apache.log (one per line, deduplicated)
exercises.hint: Use grep -oE with an IP regex pattern

exercises.prompt: Find all lines in server.log that start with a timestamp (digits)
exercises.hint: Use ^ to anchor to line start, then a digit class

quiz.question: What does the regex pattern ^[0-9]+ match?
options: Lines that start with one or more digits
quiz.answer: Lines that start with one or more digits
quiz.explanation: ^ anchors to line start, [0-9] matches digits, + means one or more.

quiz.question: Which flag enables | and + in grep?
quiz.explanation: -E enables Extended Regular Expressions, which support | (OR), + (one or more), and ? (zero or one).

lessons.title: Regex in sed & awk: Pattern Power
lessons.introduction: Regex patterns truly shine when combined with sed and awk. sed uses regex for powerful substitutions with backreferences, while awk leverages patterns for field-based filtering. Mastering regex in these tools unlocks text transformations impossible with simple grep.
lessons.purpose: Use regex patterns in sed substitutions and awk filtering with backreferences

sections.title: sed with Extended Regex
sections.content: sed -E enables extended regex in the pattern. Use () for groups, + for one-or-more, and ? for optional — all without escaping.
sections.example: sed -E 's/(ERROR|WARN): (.*)/[\1] \2/' server.log
sections.explanation: Captures the severity level and message, then rearranges the format with brackets

sections.title: Backreferences in sed
sections.content: \1, \2 etc. reference captured groups from the regex pattern. They let you rearrange, duplicate, or transform matched text.
sections.explanation: Converts dates from MM/DD/YYYY to YYYY-MM-DD format using backreferences

sections.title: awk Pattern Matching
sections.content: awk uses regex patterns in the pattern position before the action block. Match, extract, and filter based on complex patterns.
sections.explanation: Prints only lines that start with an IP address pattern

sections.title: awk Field Matching with Regex
sections.content: awk's ~ operator matches a field against a regex. !~ matches fields that don't match. Enables field-level regex filtering.
sections.example: awk -F',' '$3 ~ /^[A-C]/ {print $2, $3}' employees.csv
sections.explanation: Prints employees whose department name starts with A, B, or C

sections.title: sed Lookaround (PCRE)
sections.content: With grep -P or GNU sed with PCRE support, use (?=...) positive lookahead and (?<!...) negative lookaround.
sections.example: grep -P '(?<=user=)\w+' server.log
sections.explanation: Extracts usernames that appear after 'user=' — the lookbehind doesn't consume the prefix

sections.title: Complex sed Transformations
sections.content: Combine multiple regex substitutions, backreferences, and address ranges for complex text transformations.
sections.explanation: Wraps numbers in brackets and merges consecutive bracketed numbers with dots

common_mistakes: Using sed without -E for extended regex — \( \) needed for groups instead of ( )
Forgetting that awk's ~ matches the WHOLE field, not just a substring — use .* for partial matches
Confusing \1 (backreference in replacement) with \1 (group in pattern) — context matters
best_practices: Use sed -E consistently to avoid confusion between basic and extended regex syntax
Build complex sed patterns incrementally — test each substitution separately first
Use awk /pattern/ for whole-line matching and $field ~ /pattern/ for field-level matching

exercises.prompt: In employees.csv, swap columns 2 and 3 (name and department) using sed
exercises.hint: Capture three comma-separated fields and rearrange their order

exercises.prompt: From server.log, print only lines where field 2 contains at least 5 digits
exercises.hint: Use awk field regex matching with {5,} quantifier

quiz.question: In sed replacement, what does \1 refer to?
options: The first file in the argument list
The text matched by the first captured group in the pattern
The first line of the file
The first character of the match
quiz.answer: The text matched by the first captured group in the pattern
quiz.explanation: Backreferences in the replacement string refer to captured groups: \1 is group 1, \2 is group 2, etc.

quiz.question: In awk, to match field 2 against a regex, use ___
quiz.explanation: The ~ operator in awk tests if a field matches a regex pattern. !~ tests for non-match.

tracks.name: Shell Pipelines
tracks.description: Compose powerful data pipelines by chaining Unix commands.

lessons.title: Pipelines: The Unix Philosophy
lessons.introduction: The pipe (|) is one of the most powerful ideas in computing: take the output of one command and feed it as input to another. This lets you compose small, focused tools into powerful data processing pipelines — no programming required.
lessons.purpose: Chain commands so stdout of one becomes stdin of the next

sections.title: The Pipe Operator
sections.content: | passes stdout of the left command to stdin of the right. Commands run concurrently — data streams through.
sections.example: cat server.log | grep ERROR | wc -l
sections.explanation: Count error lines: read file → filter errors → count

sections.title: Building Step by Step
sections.content: Always build pipelines incrementally. Run each step, verify output, add the next.
sections.example: awk '{print $1}' apache.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10
sections.explanation: Top 10 IPs: extract → sort → count → re-sort → limit

sections.title: Redirection: > and >>
sections.content: > redirects output to a file (overwrites). >> appends. < reads stdin from a file.
sections.example: grep ERROR server.log > errors_only.txt
sections.explanation: Save all error lines to a separate file for later analysis

sections.title: tee: Split the Stream
sections.content: tee writes to both stdout AND a file simultaneously. See output while saving it.
sections.example: grep ERROR server.log | tee errors.txt | wc -l
sections.explanation: Saves errors to file AND prints the count to terminal

sections.title: xargs: Distribute Arguments
sections.content: xargs takes stdin and passes items as arguments to another command.
sections.example: grep -l ERROR *.log | xargs wc -l
sections.explanation: Count lines in every log file that contains errors

common_mistakes: Piping to a command that doesn't read stdin (use xargs instead)
Overwriting a file you're reading: cat file | grep x > file empties it!
Missing quotes around patterns with spaces or special characters
best_practices: Build and test each stage before adding the next
Use tee to save intermediate results while debugging
Document complex pipelines with comments in a script

exercises.prompt: Count how many unique IPs are in apache.log
exercises.hint: Extract IPs, deduplicate, then count

exercises.prompt: Show the 5 most common words in server.log
exercises.solution: cat server.log | tr -s '[:space:]' '\n' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
exercises.hint: Split to words, sort, count, re-sort, limit to 5

quiz.question: What does the > operator do?
quiz.explanation: > redirects stdout to a file, overwriting it. >> appends. | pipes to another command. < reads from file.

lessons.title: find & xargs: Filesystem Mastery
lessons.introduction: find and xargs together let you locate files by any criteria and apply operations to them in bulk — one of the most powerful combinations in the Unix toolbox.
lessons.purpose: Locate files and apply bulk operations using find and xargs

sections.title: find by Name
sections.content: Find files matching a name pattern anywhere in the directory tree.
sections.example: find . -name '*.log'
sections.explanation: Recursively finds all .log files from current directory

sections.title: find by Type
sections.content: -type f for files, -type d for directories.
sections.example: find . -type f -name '*.csv'
sections.explanation: Only files named *.csv, not directories

sections.title: find by Size
sections.content: -size finds files above/below a size. +10M means over 10 megabytes.
sections.example: find . -size +1M -type f
sections.explanation: Find all files over 1MB — useful for disk cleanup

sections.title: find by Time
sections.content: -mtime -1 means modified in the last day. -newer FILE means newer than a reference file.
sections.example: find . -mtime -1 -name '*.log'
sections.explanation: Find log files modified today

sections.title: xargs: Batch Processing
sections.content: xargs converts stdin lines to arguments for another command.
sections.example: find . -name '*.log' | xargs wc -l
sections.explanation: Count lines in every log file found

sections.title: xargs with Spaces
sections.content: Use -print0 with find and -0 with xargs to handle filenames with spaces.
sections.example: find . -name '*.log' -print0 | xargs -0 grep -l ERROR
sections.explanation: Safely process log files even if they have spaces in names

common_mistakes: Using find without -maxdepth on huge directory trees
Forgetting -print0 / -0 for filenames with spaces
find . -name *.log without quotes — shell expands * before find sees it
best_practices: Always quote patterns: find . -name '*.log' not *.log
Use find ... -exec cmd {} + for performance (batches args like xargs)
Add -maxdepth 2 to limit recursion depth on large trees

exercises.prompt: Find all files in the workspace directory and count how many there are
exercises.hint: find -type f lists files, pipe to wc -l

quiz.question: What does find . -mtime -1 find?
options: Files modified in the last 24 hours
quiz.answer: Files modified in the last 24 hours
quiz.explanation: -mtime -1 means 'modified less than 1 day ago' — the minus sign means 'less than N days'.

lessons.title: Advanced Pipelines: Process Substitution & Beyond
lessons.introduction: Beyond simple pipes, bash offers process substitution, coprocesses, and named pipes for more flexible data flow. These advanced techniques let you compare command outputs, run parallel processes, and create complex data flows that simple pipes can't handle.
lessons.purpose: Build advanced data flows with process substitution, coprocesses, and named pipes

sections.title: Process Substitution
sections.content: <(cmd) replaces the command's stdout with a file descriptor. Lets you use command output as if it were a file — without temp files or subshells.
sections.example: diff <(sort file1.txt) <(sort file2.txt)
sections.explanation: Compares two files after sorting, without creating temporary sorted files

sections.title: Comparing with Process Substitution
sections.content: Process substitution shines for comparing outputs of different commands side by side.
sections.example: diff <(awk '{print $1}' apache.log | sort -u) <(awk '{print $1}' nginx.log | sort -u)
sections.explanation: Compares unique IPs between Apache and nginx logs

sections.title: Named Pipes (FIFOs)
sections.content: mkfifo creates a named pipe — a persistent file that acts as a data channel between processes. Data written to a FIFO blocks until something reads it.
sections.example:
mkfifo /tmp/mypipe
# Terminal 1: writer
echo 'hello' > /tmp/mypipe
# Terminal 2: reader
cat /tmp/mypipe
sections.explanation: Named pipes enable inter-process communication. The writer blocks until the reader opens the pipe.

sections.title: Named Pipes for Workflows
sections.content: Use FIFOs to connect producer and consumer scripts without temp files. Clean up with rm when done.
sections.example:
mkfifo /tmp/data_pipe
awk '{print $1, $4}' apache.log > /tmp/data_pipe &
while read ip bytes; do
  echo "$ip transferred $bytes bytes"
done < /tmp/data_pipe
rm /tmp/data_pipe
sections.explanation: Producer feeds extracted data into the pipe, consumer processes it line by line

sections.title: Coprocesses
sections.content: coproc runs a command in the background with its stdin/stdout connected to the parent shell. Read from and write to the coprocess.
sections.example:
coproc BC
for i in $(seq 1 10); do
  echo "$i * $i" >&${BC[1]}
  read result <&${BC[0]}
  echo "$i squared = $result"
done
kill $BC_PID
sections.explanation: Runs bc as a coprocess, sending calculations and reading results interactively

sections.title: Parallel Execution Patterns
sections.content: Use background processes with wait for parallelism. Process substitution feeds multiple consumers simultaneously.
sections.example:
for logfile in *.log; do
  (grep -c ERROR "$logfile" > "/tmp/count_$logfile") &
done
wait
cat /tmp/count_*
sections.explanation: Counts errors in each log file in parallel, then collects results after all finish

common_mistakes: Forgetting to clean up named pipes with rm — they persist as files on disk
Using process substitution when a simple pipe would suffice — overcomplicating
Not waiting for background processes before reading results — race conditions
best_practices: Use process substitution <(cmd) instead of temp files for comparing command outputs
Always rm named pipes when done — they're files, not automatically cleaned up
Use wait to synchronize background processes before collecting their output

exercises.prompt: Compare unique IP addresses between apache.log and nginx.log using process substitution
exercises.hint: Use <(cmd) process substitution with diff

exercises.prompt: Create a named pipe and write the word count of server.log through it
exercises.solution:
mkfifo /tmp/wc_pipe
wc -l < server.log > /tmp/wc_pipe &
read lines < /tmp/wc_pipe
echo "Lines: $lines"
rm /tmp/wc_pipe
exercises.hint: Use mkfifo to create the pipe, write to it in background, read from it

quiz.question: What does <(sort file.txt) do in bash?
options: Creates a temporary file with sorted content
Creates a process substitution that acts as a file with sorted output
Creates a symlink to sorted output
quiz.answer: Creates a process substitution that acts as a file with sorted output
quiz.explanation: Process substitution <(cmd) creates a file descriptor connected to the command's stdout, usable anywhere a filename is expected.

quiz.question: To create a named pipe, use command ___
quiz.explanation: mkfifo creates a FIFO (named pipe) — a special file that acts as a data channel between processes.

tracks.name: Log Analysis
tracks.description: Real-world log parsing: Apache, Nginx, syslog, and application logs.

lessons.title: Log Analysis: Reading System Stories
lessons.introduction: Logs are the heartbeat of every system. Learning to parse them with command-line tools is a superpower — you can diagnose incidents, find security issues, and understand system behavior without any specialized tools.
lessons.purpose: Parse Apache, Nginx, syslog, and custom application logs
lessons.syntax: grep | awk | sed | sort | uniq applied to structured log files

sections.title: Apache Combined Log Format
sections.content: Apache logs follow: IP - - [datetime] "METHOD URL protocol" status bytes "referer" "user-agent"
sections.example: awk '{print $1,$7,$9}' apache.log | head -5
sections.explanation: Extracts IP, URL, and status code from the first 5 lines

sections.title: Counting Status Codes
sections.content: Quick health check: what response codes is your server sending?
sections.example: awk '{print $9}' apache.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
sections.explanation: Distribution of all HTTP status codes — 200s are good, 500s are errors

sections.title: Traffic Analysis
sections.content: Find peak traffic periods and most popular content.
sections.example: awk '{print $4}' apache.log | cut -d: -f2 | sort | uniq -c
sections.explanation: Request count per hour of day

sections.title: Error Investigation
sections.content: Find and count 404 errors — missing pages that need fixing.
sections.example: awk '$9==404 {print $7}' apache.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10
sections.explanation: Top 10 missing URLs — could be a broken link or a probing attack

sections.title: syslog Format
sections.content: syslog format: Month Day HH:MM:SS hostname process[pid]: message
sections.example: grep 'error' syslog.log | awk '{print $1,$2,$5}' | sort | uniq -c
sections.explanation: Error frequency by service

sections.title: Bandwidth Analysis
sections.content: Calculate total bytes transferred from Apache log field 10.
sections.example: awk '{sum+=$10} END {printf "Total: %.2f MB\n", sum/1048576}' apache.log
sections.explanation: Total bandwidth served — useful for billing and capacity planning

common_mistakes: Forgetting that Apache field numbers shift if your log format differs
Treating IP::port as just IP without extracting the IP part
Not handling log rotation — yesterday's log is in a .1 or .gz file
best_practices: Build a library of one-liners for your most common queries
Use awk BEGIN to print headers for your reports
Cross-reference multiple log files to correlate events

exercises.prompt: Find the top 3 most requested URLs in apache.log
exercises.solution: awk '{print $7}' apache.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3
exercises.hint: Field 7 is the URL, then sort|uniq|sort|head

exercises.prompt: Count total 500 errors in apache.log
exercises.hint: Filter where field 9 equals 500, then count

quiz.question: In Apache Combined Log Format, which field contains the HTTP status code?
quiz.explanation: The standard Apache Combined Log Format: IP - - [timestamp] "request" STATUS bytes "referer" "user-agent". Status is field 9.

lessons.title: Advanced Log Analysis: Incident Response
lessons.introduction: When systems go wrong, the logs tell the story. Advanced log analysis combines pattern matching, time correlation, and multi-file analysis to diagnose incidents in minutes rather than hours.
lessons.purpose: Correlate events across log files and detect anomalies

sections.title: Time Windowing
sections.content: Extract events in a specific time window using awk comparisons on the timestamp field.
sections.example: awk '$4~/14:[0-5][0-9]:/ {print}' apache.log | wc -l
sections.explanation: Count requests during the 14:00–14:59 hour (2 PM)

sections.title: Anomaly Detection
sections.content: Spot IPs with unusually high request rates — a sign of bots or attacks.
sections.example: awk '{count[$1]++} END {for(ip in count) if(count[ip]>100) print ip, count[ip]}' apache.log
sections.explanation: Lists any IP with over 100 requests — potential threat

sections.title: Error Rate Trending
sections.content: Calculate error rates over time to spot degradation.
sections.example: awk '{total++; if($9>=500) errors++} END {printf "Error rate: %.1f%%\n", errors/total*100}' apache.log
sections.explanation: Overall 5xx error rate — the key SLO metric

sections.title: Multi-Log Correlation
sections.content: Combine apache and nginx logs for a unified view.
sections.example: cat apache.log nginx.log | sort -k4 | grep 'ERROR\|500' | tail -50
sections.explanation: Unified error timeline across both web servers

sections.title: Failed Login Detection
sections.content: Find repeated authentication failures — brute force attacks leave a pattern.
sections.example: grep 'authentication failure\|Failed password' syslog.log | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10
sections.explanation: Top 10 users targeted by auth failures

sections.title: Reporting with awk
sections.content: Generate a proper incident report with awk's printf.
sections.example: awk '{errors[$9]++} END {print "=== Error Report ==="; for(s in errors) if(s>=400) printf "%s: %d\n", s, errors[s]}' apache.log | sort
sections.explanation: Formatted error report showing all HTTP error codes and counts

common_mistakes: Looking at logs in isolation — always correlate with other log sources
Forgetting timezone differences when correlating logs from different systems
Sampling logs without understanding sampling bias
best_practices: Archive raw logs before analysis — you may need to re-examine them
Save your one-liners to a runbook for the next incident
Always check log file sizes before cat-ing — use head first

exercises.prompt: Calculate the 5xx error rate as a percentage in apache.log
exercises.solution: awk '{t++; if($9>=500) e++} END {printf "%.1f%%\n", e/t*100}' apache.log
exercises.hint: Count total and errors separately, compute percentage in END

quiz.question: You want to find IPs making more than 50 requests. Where does the filter go in awk?
options: In an END block after counting
quiz.answer: In an END block after counting
quiz.explanation: You must count ALL requests per IP first (using an array), then filter in END where totals are available.

tracks.name: VLSI Text Processing
tracks.description: Parse VLSI EDA tool reports: timing, synthesis, liberty, and constraints.

lessons.title: VLSI Reports: EDA Text Processing
lessons.introduction: VLSI design tools generate massive text reports. Physical design engineers spend significant time parsing timing reports, synthesis logs, and liberty files. Command-line tools turn hours of manual searching into seconds of automated extraction.
lessons.purpose: Parse EDA tool outputs: timing reports, synthesis logs, SDC, Liberty
lessons.syntax: grep | awk | sed applied to EDA report formats

sections.title: Timing Reports
sections.content: Timing reports show setup/hold slack for each path. Negative slack = violation.
sections.example: grep 'VIOLATED' timing.rpt | wc -l
sections.explanation: Quick count of timing violations — the number every PE watches

sections.title: Worst Negative Slack
sections.content: Find the critical path — the path with the worst (most negative) slack.
sections.example: grep 'slack' timing.rpt | grep -oE '[-0-9.]+' | sort -n | head -1
sections.explanation: Extracts the WNS — the number that defines your achievable frequency

sections.title: Liberty File Parsing
sections.content: Liberty files define cell timing and power. Counting cells, pins, and attributes.
sections.example: grep -c '^\s*cell' liberty.lib
sections.explanation: Total standard cells in the library

sections.title: SDC Constraint Analysis
sections.content: SDC files define timing constraints. Extract clock definitions and frequencies.
sections.example: grep 'create_clock' constraints.sdc | awk '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) if($i=="-period") print $(i+1)}'
sections.explanation: Extracts all clock periods (divide 1000 to get MHz)

sections.title: Synthesis Report Mining
sections.content: Synthesis logs contain area, power, and QoR summaries buried in verbose output.
sections.example: awk '/Cell Area/,/^$/' synthesis.log | head -20
sections.explanation: Extracts the cell area section from synthesis report

sections.title: Netlist Statistics
sections.content: Count cells, instances, and connections in a Verilog netlist.
sections.example: grep -c '^\s*\.' netlist.v
sections.explanation: Count module port connections — proxy for design size

common_mistakes: EDA reports often have leading whitespace — use \s* or trim before comparing
Numbers may be in scientific notation (1.23e-09) — handle with awk
Report format changes between tool versions — always verify column positions
best_practices: Build a library of EDA parsing scripts versioned with your design
Use awk for multi-field extraction from tabular EDA reports
Cross-check extracted numbers against the tool's own summary report

exercises.prompt: Count the number of timing violations (VIOLATED) in timing.rpt
exercises.hint: grep -c counts matching lines

exercises.prompt: List all clock names defined in constraints.sdc
exercises.hint: Look for -name argument in create_clock statements

quiz.question: What does negative slack in a timing report mean?
options: The path has a timing violation
quiz.answer: The path has a timing violation
quiz.explanation: Negative slack means the signal arrives late — the timing constraint is violated. The design cannot run at the target frequency.

tracks.name: Shell Scripting
tracks.description: Write effective shell scripts with variables, control flow, functions, and advanced techniques.

lessons.title: Shell Scripting: From Commands to Programs
lessons.introduction: Shell scripting transforms one-off commands into reusable programs. By combining variables, conditionals, loops, and functions, you can automate repetitive tasks, build data pipelines, and create system administration tools — all within the shell.
lessons.purpose: Automate tasks by combining shell commands into reusable scripts

sections.title: Shebang and Script Basics
sections.content: Every script starts with #!/bin/bash (the shebang). Make scripts executable with chmod +x. Variables are assigned without spaces: name=value and referenced with $name or ${name}.
sections.explanation: The shebang tells the system which interpreter to use. No spaces around = in assignment. ${name} references the variable.

sections.title: Conditional Statements
sections.content: Use if/elif/else for branching. Test conditions with [ ] (test) or [[ ]] (bash extended). Common tests: -f (file exists), -d (directory exists), -z (empty string), -eq (equals).
sections.example:
if [ -f server.log ]; then
  echo "Log file exists"
  wc -l < server.log
else
  echo "No log file found"
fi
sections.explanation: -f tests if a regular file exists. The script checks for server.log and counts its lines if found.

sections.title: For Loops
sections.content: for loops iterate over lists, command outputs, or ranges. Use for VAR in LIST; do ... done.
sections.example:
for file in *.log; do
  echo "$file: $(wc -l < "$file") lines"
done
sections.explanation: Iterates over all .log files in the current directory and prints each file's line count.

sections.title: While Loops
sections.content: while loops continue as long as a condition is true. Perfect for reading files line by line or retrying operations.
sections.example:
while IFS=',' read -r name dept salary; do
  echo "$name works in $dept"
done < employees.csv
sections.explanation: Reads employees.csv line by line, splitting on commas into three variables. IFS sets the field separator.

sections.title: Functions
sections.content: Functions group reusable logic. Define with function name() { ... } or name() { ... }. Return values via echo and command substitution $(function_name).
sections.explanation: Function takes a filename argument, counts ERROR lines, returns 0 if grep fails. Local variable scope with 'local'.

sections.title: Command-Line Arguments
sections.content: $1, $2, ... are positional parameters. $# is the argument count. $@ represents all arguments. Use shift to consume arguments one at a time.
sections.example:
if [ $# -lt 2 ]; then
  echo "Usage: $0 <file> <pattern>"
  exit 1
fi
grep -c "$2" "$1"
sections.explanation: Checks that at least 2 arguments were provided, then counts pattern matches in the file.

common_mistakes: Forgetting to make scripts executable: chmod +x script.sh
Using spaces around = in variable assignment: name = value is WRONG
Not quoting variables: $file breaks on filenames with spaces — use "$file"
Using [ ] instead of [[ ]] for pattern matching — [[ ]] supports glob patterns natively
best_practices: Always quote variables: "$var" prevents word splitting and glob expansion
Use local for function variables to avoid polluting global scope
Set -e at the top to exit on any error (set -euo pipefail for production scripts)
Add a usage message when scripts require arguments

exercises.prompt: Write a script that counts ERROR, WARN, and INFO lines in server.log
exercises.solution:
echo "ERROR: $(grep -c 'ERROR' server.log)"
echo "WARN: $(grep -c 'WARN' server.log)"
echo "INFO: $(grep -c 'INFO' server.log)"
exercises.hint: Use grep -c for each severity level

exercises.prompt: Write a for loop that prints each CSV file in the workspace and its line count
exercises.solution: for f in *.csv; do echo "$f: $(wc -l < "$f") lines"; done
exercises.hint: Use for FILE in *.csv with wc -l

exercises.prompt: Write a function that takes a directory name and lists all .log files in it
exercises.hint: Use find with -name and -type f

quiz.question: What does #!/bin/bash at the top of a script do?
options: Tells the system which interpreter to use
quiz.answer: Tells the system which interpreter to use
quiz.explanation: The shebang (#!) tells the kernel which program to use to interpret the script.

quiz.question: To count the number of arguments passed to a script, use variable ___
quiz.explanation: $# holds the count of positional parameters (arguments). $1, $2 etc. are the actual arguments.

quiz.question: Which keyword declares a function-local variable?
quiz.explanation: local restricts a variable's scope to the current function. Without it, the variable is global.

lessons.title: Advanced Shell Scripting
lessons.introduction: Advanced shell scripting unlocks arrays, string manipulation, signal handling with trap, and option parsing with getopts. These features let you write robust, production-quality scripts that handle errors gracefully and accept complex command-line interfaces.
lessons.purpose: Write production-quality scripts with arrays, error handling, and option parsing
lessons.syntax: array=(a b c); ${array[@]}; ${#string}; trap 'cmd' SIGNAL; getopts opt: var

sections.title: Arrays
sections.content: Bash arrays are zero-indexed. Declare with arr=(values). Access elements with ${arr[0]}, all elements with ${arr[@]}, and length with ${#arr[@]}.
sections.example:
files=(server.log apache.log syslog.log)
for f in "${files[@]}"; do
  echo "$f: $(wc -l < "$f") lines"
done
sections.explanation: Creates an array of log files and iterates over all of them. Quotes around ${arr[@]} preserve spaces.

sections.title: String Manipulation
sections.content: Bash provides parameter expansion for string operations: ${var%pattern} (remove suffix), ${var#pattern} (remove prefix), ${var//old/new} (replace all), ${var:offset:length} (substring).
sections.example:
filename="server.log.bak"
echo "Base: ${filename%.}"          # server.log.bak (no change)
echo "Name: ${filename%.*}"         # server.log
echo "Ext: ${filename##*.}"         # bak
echo "Upper: ${filename^^}"         # SERVER.LOG.BAK
sections.explanation: %.* removes the shortest suffix matching .* (the extension). ##*. removes the longest prefix matching *. (everything before the last dot).

sections.title: Trap: Signal Handling
sections.content: trap catches signals (EXIT, INT, TERM, ERR) and runs cleanup code. Essential for scripts that create temporary files.
sections.example:
tmpfile=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$tmpfile"' EXIT
process_data > "$tmpfile"
# script exits — trap fires, temp file is cleaned up
sections.explanation: The EXIT trap fires no matter how the script exits (normal, error, or signal). This prevents orphaned temp files.

sections.title: getopts: Option Parsing
sections.content: getopts parses short options (-v -f file). The optstring defines valid options; a colon after a letter means it requires an argument.
sections.explanation: Parses -v (flag), -f and -o (options with arguments). OPTARG holds the argument value for options with colons.

sections.title: Debugging Scripts
sections.content: Use set -x to trace execution (prints each command before running). set -e exits on error. set -u treats unset variables as errors.
sections.example:
set -euo pipefail
# Your script runs with strict error handling
# -e: exit on error
# -u: error on unset variable
# -o pipefail: catch errors in piped commands
sections.explanation: set -euo pipefail is the gold standard for robust scripts. It catches three classes of bugs automatically.

sections.title: Here Documents and Here Strings
sections.content: Here documents (<<EOF) pass multi-line input to commands. Here strings (<<<) pass a single string as stdin.
sections.example:
grep -c 'ERROR' server.log | awk '{print "Error count:", $1}' <<< "$(cat <<EOF
WARNING: disk space low
ERROR: connection refused
INFO: backup complete
EOF
)"
sections.explanation: Here documents provide multi-line input inline. Here strings feed a string to a command's stdin.

common_mistakes: Forgetting to quote ${arr[@]} — unquoted expansion splits on spaces
Using trap without quoting the command — single quotes prevent variable expansion at define time
Not resetting OPTIND when parsing options in a loop
Using set -e without understanding it skips errors in conditionals (if cmd; then)
best_practices: Always use set -euo pipefail in production scripts
Clean up temp files with trap EXIT — never rely on normal exit paths
Use arrays instead of space-separated strings for lists of items
Document options with a usage function, not just getopts

exercises.prompt: Write a script that accepts -f FILE and -n COUNT arguments and prints the first COUNT lines of FILE
exercises.solution:
while getopts f:n: opt; do
  case $opt in
    f) file="$OPTARG" ;;
    n) count="$OPTARG" ;;
  esac
done
head -"$count" "$file"
exercises.hint: Use getopts with f: and n: to parse options with arguments

exercises.prompt: Write a trap that removes all .tmp files when a script exits
exercises.solution:
trap 'rm -f *.tmp' EXIT
echo "working" > temp1.tmp
echo "done" > temp2.tmp
exercises.hint: Use trap with EXIT signal

quiz.question: What does ${var%%.*} do?
quiz.explanation: %% removes the longest suffix matching the pattern. % removes the shortest. For file.txt, %%.* gives file, %.* gives file.txt (wrong for multiple dots).

quiz.question: To catch errors and run cleanup when a script exits, use trap with signal ___
quiz.explanation: trap 'cleanup' EXIT runs cleanup no matter how the script exits — normal, error, or killed by signal.

lessons.title: Trap & Debug: Signal Handling & Script Debugging
lessons.introduction: Production scripts must handle signals gracefully, clean up resources on failure, and provide debugging capabilities. The trap command intercepts signals and errors, while set -x and trap DEBUG provide visibility into script execution.
lessons.purpose: Handle signals, clean up on errors, and debug scripts with trap and tracing

sections.title: Basic Trap: EXIT
sections.content: trap 'cleanup' EXIT runs cleanup when the script exits — whether normally, on error, or by signal. Essential for temp file cleanup.
sections.example:
tmpfile=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$tmpfile"' EXIT
process_data > "$tmpfile"
sections.explanation: The EXIT trap fires no matter how the script terminates — guarantees temp file cleanup

sections.title: Trapping Signals
sections.content: Trap specific signals: INT (Ctrl+C), TERM (kill), HUP (hangup). Each can trigger different cleanup actions.
sections.example:
trap 'echo "Interrupted!"; exit 1' INT
trap 'echo "Terminated"; cleanup; exit 0' TERM
while true; do process; done
sections.explanation: Custom handlers for each signal — INT prints a message, TERM runs cleanup first

sections.title: ERR Trap for Error Handling
sections.content: trap 'cmd' ERR fires when any command returns a non-zero status. Combined with set -e, it provides automatic error handling.
sections.example:
set -e
trap 'echo "Error on line $LINENO" >&2' ERR
rm /nonexistent/file
sections.explanation: When the rm command fails, the ERR trap fires with the line number for debugging

sections.title: DEBUG Trap for Tracing
sections.content: trap 'cmd' DEBUG runs before every command. Useful for logging, profiling, or step-by-step debugging.
sections.example:
trap 'echo "[DEBUG] $BASH_COMMAND" >&2' DEBUG
# Every command will be printed before execution
sections.explanation: Logs every command before it runs — like set -x but customizable output

sections.title: set -x and set -e
sections.content: set -x traces execution (prints each command). set -e exits on error. set -u errors on unset variables. set -o pipefail catches pipe errors.
sections.example:
set -euo pipefail
# -e: exit on error
# -u: error on unset variable
# -o pipefail: catch errors in pipes
sections.explanation: set -euo pipefail is the gold standard for robust production scripts

sections.title: LINENO and Error Reporting
sections.content: $LINENO contains the current line number. Combine with trap for precise error location reporting.
sections.example:
trap 'echo "FAILED at line $LINENO: $BASH_COMMAND" >&2; exit 1' ERR
process_data || { echo "Data processing failed"; exit 1; }
sections.explanation: Reports the exact line and command that failed — invaluable for debugging

common_mistakes: Using trap without single quotes — double quotes expand variables at definition time, not execution time
Forgetting that set -e skips errors in conditionals (if cmd; then) — this is expected behavior
Not resetting trap for functions that handle their own errors
Using set -e without understanding interaction with subshells and pipes
best_practices: Always use trap 'cleanup' EXIT for temp files — never rely on normal exit paths
Start production scripts with set -euo pipefail for maximum safety
Use single quotes in trap commands to defer variable expansion until execution
Combine LINENO with ERR trap for precise error location in scripts

exercises.prompt: Write a script that creates a temp file, sets a trap to clean it up on EXIT, and writes data to it
exercises.solution:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
tmpfile=$(mktemp)
trap 'rm -f "$tmpfile"' EXIT
echo "Processing data..." > "$tmpfile"
cat "$tmpfile"
echo "Temp file will be cleaned up automatically"
exercises.hint: Use mktemp, trap EXIT, and do work between them

exercises.prompt: Write a script that uses trap to catch Ctrl+C (INT signal) and print a message before exiting
exercises.solution:
#!/bin/bash
trap 'echo "Caught Ctrl+C, cleaning up..."; exit 1' INT
while true; do
  echo "Working..."
  sleep 1
done
exercises.hint: Use trap with INT signal for Ctrl+C handling

quiz.question: What does set -euo pipefail do?
options: Enables strict error handling: exit on error, unset variable error, and pipe failure detection
quiz.answer: Enables strict error handling: exit on error, unset variable error, and pipe failure detection
quiz.explanation: -e exits on error, -u errors on unset vars, -o pipefail catches pipe failures. The standard for robust scripts.

quiz.question: To trace each command before execution, use set ___
quiz.explanation: set -x enables xtrace mode — each command is printed (prefixed with +) before execution. Essential for debugging.

tracks.name: File System & Permissions
tracks.description: Understand Linux file permissions, disk management, and advanced file searching.

lessons.title: File Permissions: Access Control Mastery
lessons.introduction: Linux file permissions control who can read, write, and execute files. Understanding chmod, chown, chgrp, and umask is essential for system security and for solving 'Permission denied' errors that every Linux user encounters.
lessons.purpose: Control file access with chmod, chown, and understand permission bits

sections.title: Reading Permissions
sections.content: ls -l shows permissions as rwxrwxrwx (owner, group, others). r=read(4), w=write(2), x=execute(1). Dashes (-) mean the permission is denied.
sections.example:
ls -l employees.csv
# -rw-r--r-- 1 user group 1024 Jul 20 10:00 employees.csv
sections.explanation: Owner can read+write (6), group can read (4), others can read (4). That's 644 in octal.

sections.title: chmod: Changing Permissions
sections.content: chmod sets permissions using octal (755) or symbolic (u+x, g-w) modes. Octal: owner|group|others, each digit = r(4)+w(2)+x(1).
sections.example:
chmod 755 script.sh      # rwxr-xr-x (owner full, others read+execute)
chmod 644 config.txt     # rw-r--r-- (owner read+write, others read)
chmod u+x deploy.sh      # add execute for owner only
sections.explanation: 755 is standard for executables. 644 is standard for data files. u+x adds execute to the user/owner.

sections.title: chown and chgrp
sections.content: chown changes file ownership. chgrp changes group ownership. Both require root (or sudo).
sections.example:
sudo chown www-data:www-data /var/www/html/
sudo chgrp developers project/
ls -ld /var/www/html/
sections.explanation: Sets both owner and group to www-data. Useful for web server directories where the server process needs specific ownership.

sections.title: umask: Default Permissions
sections.content: umask sets the default permission mask for new files. Default umask 022 means files get 644 and directories get 755. umask subtracts from the maximum (666 for files, 777 for dirs).
sections.example:
umask
# 0022
touch testfile && ls -l testfile
# -rw-r--r-- (666 - 022 = 644)
rm testfile
sections.explanation: umask 022 strips write for group and others from new files. This is the safe default on most systems.

sections.title: Special Permission Bits
sections.content: setuid (4) runs executables as the file owner. setgid (2) runs as the file's group. sticky bit (1) prevents deletion by non-owners (like /tmp).
sections.example:
chmod u+s /usr/bin/passwd    # setuid — runs as root
chmod g+s project/           # setgid — new files inherit group
chmod +t /shared/            # sticky bit — only owner can delete
sections.explanation: setuid is how passwd changes /etc/shadow. setgid ensures team directories stay in the right group. Sticky bit protects shared directories.

sections.title: File Type Bits
sections.content: The first character of ls -l indicates file type: - (regular file), d (directory), l (symlink), c (character device), b (block device), p (pipe), s (socket).
sections.example:
ls -ld /dev/sda /dev/tty /tmp /dev/null
# brw-rw---- block device
# crw-rw---- character device
# drwxrwxrwt directory (sticky bit)
crw-rw-rw- character device (null)
sections.explanation: Understanding file types helps identify special files. /dev/null is a character device that discards all input.

common_mistakes: chmod 777 on everything — this is a security disaster, everyone can write
Using chown without sudo — only root can change file ownership
Confusing -x on a directory (can cd into it) with -x on a file (can execute it)
Forgetting that umask is subtractive — umask 777 creates nothing writable
best_practices: Use 644 for data files, 755 for executables, 600 for private files
Never set 777 unless you fully understand the security implications
Use symbolic mode for targeted changes: chmod u+x instead of recomputing octal
Check permissions with ls -la when debugging 'Permission denied' errors

exercises.prompt: Set permissions on server.log so only the owner can read and write, and nobody else has any access
exercises.hint: 600 = rw------- (owner read+write, group and others nothing)

exercises.prompt: Show the current umask and explain what default permissions new files get
exercises.hint: umask shows the current mask. Default file permissions are 666 minus umask.

exercises.prompt: Add execute permission for the owner and group on deploy.sh, but keep others without execute
exercises.hint: Use symbolic mode with ug+ to add execute for user and group

quiz.question: What does chmod 644 mean?
options: Owner: rwx, Group: r-x, Others: r-x
Owner: rw-, Group: r--, Others: r--
Owner: rw-, Group: rw-, Others: r--
quiz.answer: Owner: rw-, Group: r--, Others: r--
quiz.explanation: 6=4+2 (read+write), 4=read only, 4=read only. Standard for data files.

quiz.question: The ___ command changes the owner of a file
quiz.explanation: chown (change owner) modifies file ownership. Requires root. chgrp changes group only.

quiz.question: What does the sticky bit do on a directory?
options: Only the file owner can delete files in that directory
quiz.answer: Only the file owner can delete files in that directory
quiz.explanation: The sticky bit (chmod +t) prevents users from deleting files they don't own. /tmp uses this to prevent users from deleting each other's temp files.

lessons.title: Disk & Storage Management
lessons.introduction: Managing disk space is a critical system administration task. Tools like df, du, mount, and lsblk let you monitor usage, find space hogs, and manage storage devices — keeping systems running smoothly.
lessons.purpose: Monitor disk usage, manage mounts, and identify space-consuming files

sections.title: df: Filesystem Space
sections.content: df shows disk space for mounted filesystems. -h gives human-readable sizes (KB/MB/GB). -T shows filesystem type.
sections.example:
df -hT
# Filesystem     Type   Size  Used Avail Use%
# /dev/sda1      ext4   50G   35G   13G  73%
sections.explanation: Quick overview of all mounted filesystems. Use this first when a system reports 'no space left on device'.

sections.title: du: Directory Usage
sections.content: du estimates file/directory space usage. -s summarizes total, -h gives human-readable sizes. --max-depth limits recursion.
sections.example: du -sh /var/log/* | sort -rh | head -10
sections.explanation: Shows the 10 largest items in /var/log, sorted by size descending — quick way to find space hogs.

sections.title: Finding Large Files
sections.content: Combine find with -size to locate files exceeding a threshold. Pipe to du or ls -lh for sizes.
sections.example: find / -type f -size +100M -exec ls -lh {} \; 2>/dev/null | sort -k5 -rh | head -10
sections.explanation: Finds all files over 100MB across the entire filesystem, sorted by size. 2>/dev/null suppresses permission errors.

sections.title: lsblk: Block Devices
sections.content: lsblk lists block devices (disks, partitions) in a tree view. Shows size, mount point, and filesystem type.
sections.example:
lsblk -f
# NAME   FSTYPE LABEL  MOUNTPOINT
# sda             
# ├─sda1 ext4          /
# └─sda2 swap          [SWAP]
sections.explanation: Shows the disk partition layout and which filesystems are mounted where.

sections.title: mount and umount
sections.content: mount attaches a filesystem to a directory. umount detaches it. /etc/fstab defines persistent mounts.
sections.example:
sudo mount /dev/sdb1 /mnt/backup
mount | grep sdb
sudo umount /mnt/backup
sections.explanation: Mount a USB drive or network share to access its files. Always umount before physically removing devices.

sections.title: Inode Usage
sections.content: df -i shows inode usage. Each file consumes one inode regardless of size. Systems can run out of inodes before running out of disk space.
sections.example:
df -i
# Filesystem     Inodes   IUsed   IFree IUse% Mounted on
# /dev/sda1      3.2M    2.1M    1.1M   66% /
sections.explanation: If IUse% is 100%, you can't create new files even with free disk space. Common with millions of tiny files.

common_mistakes: Confusing df (filesystem-level) with du (file-level) — they measure different things
Not using -h flags — raw byte counts are hard to read
Forgetting 2>/dev/null on find across / — permission errors flood output
Not checking inodes — a filesystem can be 50% full by space but 100% full by inodes
best_practices: Run df -hT first when investigating disk issues, then du to drill down
Use du -sh * to find the largest items in the current directory
Add --max-depth=1 to du for a high-level overview before drilling deeper
Schedule regular cleanup of /var/log, /tmp, and package manager caches

exercises.prompt: Find the 5 largest files anywhere in the workspace directory
exercises.hint: Use find with -exec ls -s to get file sizes, then sort numerically descending

exercises.prompt: Show disk usage summary for each top-level directory in the current workspace
exercises.hint: du -sh for each directory, sort by size reverse human

quiz.question: What is the difference between df and du?
options: df shows file sizes, du shows directory sizes
df shows filesystem-level usage, du shows file/directory-level usage
df is for ext4, du is for all filesystems
quiz.answer: df shows filesystem-level usage, du shows file/directory-level usage
quiz.explanation: df reports on mounted filesystems (total/used/available). du estimates space used by files and directories.

quiz.question: To list block devices and their mount points in a tree view, use command ___
quiz.explanation: lsblk (list block devices) shows disks, partitions, filesystem types, and mount points in a visual tree.

lessons.title: Advanced find: Complex File Searches
lessons.introduction: The find command is far more than a simple filename search. With action predicates (-exec, -ok), combinations (-and, -or, -not), and integration with xargs, it becomes a powerful tool for complex filesystem operations.
lessons.purpose: Perform complex file searches with actions, predicates, and bulk operations

sections.title: Combining Tests with Boolean Logic
sections.content: find supports -and, -or, -not (or !) for complex conditions. Tests can be grouped with \( \).
sections.example: find . -type f \( -name '*.log' -o -name '*.csv' \) -size +1M
sections.explanation: Finds files that are either .log or .csv AND larger than 1MB. The grouping ensures OR applies before -size.

sections.title: exec: Running Commands on Results
sections.content: -exec runs a command for each file found. {} is replaced with the filename. + at the end batches files like xargs for efficiency.
sections.example: find . -name '*.log' -exec grep -l 'ERROR' {} +
sections.explanation: Finds all .log files and searches each for ERROR. The + batches files, running grep once with multiple filenames.

sections.title: exec vs xargs
sections.content: xargs is often faster than -exec because it can parallelize. Use -print0 with find and -0 with xargs for safe handling of spaces in filenames.
sections.example: find . -name '*.csv' -print0 | xargs -0 -I{} wc -l {}
sections.explanation: Print0/xargs-0 handles filenames with spaces safely. -I{} processes one file at a time.

sections.title: Time-Based Searches
sections.content: -mtime (modification days), -mmin (modification minutes), -newerref (newer than a reference file).
sections.example: find . -name '*.log' -mmin -60 -exec ls -la {} +
sections.explanation: Finds .log files modified in the last 60 minutes — useful for finding recently written logs.

sections.title: Permission and Ownership Searches
sections.content: -perm matches permissions. -user and -group match ownership. Useful for security audits.
sections.example:
find / -type f -perm -4000 2>/dev/null
find . -type f -user root -writable
sections.explanation: First: finds setuid files (security audit). Second: finds files owned by root that are world-writable (security risk).

sections.title: Depth and Pruning
sections.content: -maxdepth limits search depth. -prune excludes directories. -mindepth skips the starting directory itself.
sections.example: find . -maxdepth 2 -type d -name 'node_modules' -prune -o -type f -name '*.js' -print
sections.explanation: Finds .js files but skips node_modules directories. The -prune prevents descending into excluded directories.

common_mistakes: Using -name *.log without quotes — the shell expands * before find sees it
Forgetting -print0/-0 for filenames with spaces in pipelines
Using -exec cmd {} \; (runs once per file) instead of {} + (batches for efficiency)
Not using -maxdepth on large filesystems — searches can take very long
best_practices: Always quote glob patterns: -name '*.log' not -name *.log
Use {} + instead of {} \; for -exec — it batches arguments for better performance
Add 2>/dev/null to searches across / to suppress permission-denied noise
Combine -prune with -o to exclude directories without descending into them

exercises.prompt: Find all .csv files in the workspace and count the lines in each
exercises.hint: Use find with -exec and {} + for batched execution

exercises.prompt: Find all files larger than 10KB in the workspace that contain the word 'ERROR'
exercises.hint: Combine -size and -exec grep -l

exercises.prompt: Find all directories named 'logs' anywhere under the current directory
exercises.hint: Use -type d for directories only

quiz.question: What is the difference between -exec cmd {} \; and -exec cmd {} +?
options: \; runs the command once per file, + batches files into one command
+ runs the command once per file, \; batches files
quiz.answer: \; runs the command once per file, + batches files into one command
quiz.explanation: + collects as many filenames as possible into one command invocation (like xargs), while \; runs the command separately for each file.

quiz.question: To prevent find from descending into a directory, use the ___ predicate
quiz.explanation: -prune prevents find from descending into matched directories. It's used with -o to exclude specific paths.

lessons.title: File Attributes: stat, xattr & Special Bits
lessons.introduction: Beyond basic permissions, Linux files have extended attributes, special permission bits, and metadata that affect security and behavior. Understanding stat, file, xattr, and the setuid/setgid/sticky bits is essential for system administration and security auditing.
lessons.purpose: Inspect file metadata, extended attributes, and special permission bits
lessons.syntax: stat [OPTIONS] FILE  |  file [OPTIONS] FILE  |  getfattr/setfattr  |  lsattr/chattr

sections.title: stat: Detailed File Info
sections.content: stat displays comprehensive file metadata: size, permissions, timestamps, inode, links, and blocks. More detailed than ls -l.
sections.example:
stat server.log
stat -c '%a %U %G %s %n' server.log
sections.explanation: -c formats output: %a octal permissions, %U owner, %G group, %s size, %n filename

sections.title: file: File Type Detection
sections.content: file identifies the true type of a file by examining its contents (magic bytes), not just the extension.
sections.example:
file server.log
file mystery_file
file -i image.png
sections.explanation: Detects actual file type from content — a .txt file containing binary data is identified correctly

sections.title: Extended Attributes (xattr)
sections.content: Extended attributes store metadata beyond permissions: security labels, capabilities, and custom key-value pairs.
sections.example:
getfattr -d server.log
setfattr -n user.purpose -v 'log file' server.log
getfattr -n user.purpose server.log
sections.explanation: Read and set custom attributes — useful for labeling files with application metadata

sections.title: setuid and setgid Bits
sections.content: setuid (4000) runs executables as the file owner. setgid (2000) runs as the file's group. Critical for privileged operations.
sections.example:
ls -la /usr/bin/passwd
# -rwsr-xr-x 1 root root ... /usr/bin/passwd
find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
sections.explanation: passwd needs setuid to modify /etc/shadow. Finding setuid files is a security audit essential.

sections.title: Sticky Bit
sections.content: The sticky bit (1000) on directories prevents users from deleting files they don't own. Used on /tmp and shared directories.
sections.example:
ls -ld /tmp
# drwxrwxrwt 15 root root 4096 ... /tmp
chmod +t /shared/
chmod -t /shared/
sections.explanation: The 't' in the last position of permissions is the sticky bit — only file owners can delete their own files

sections.title: Filesystem Attributes (chattr/lsattr)
sections.content: Linux-specific attributes like immutable (i), append-only (a), and compressed (c) are set with chattr and viewed with lsattr.
sections.example:
lsattr important.conf
sudo chattr +i important.conf  # make immutable
sudo chattr -i important.conf  # remove immutable
