sections.explanation: Immutable files cannot be modified, deleted, or renamed — even by root — until the attribute is removed

common_mistakes: Confusing setuid on a file (runs as owner) with setgid on a file (runs as group)
Not auditing setuid files regularly — they're a common security risk if misconfigured
Using chattr +i and forgetting to remove it — even root can't modify the file until -i is used
best_practices: Regularly audit setuid/setgid files with find / -perm -4000
Use stat -c for machine-readable file metadata in scripts
Use file command to verify file types before processing — don't trust extensions
Use immutable bit on critical config files to prevent accidental modification

exercises.prompt: Show the octal permissions, owner, group, and size of server.log using stat
exercises.hint: Use stat -c with format specifiers %a %U %G %s

exercises.prompt: Find all setuid files on the system (first 10 results)
exercises.hint: Use find with -perm -4000 to match setuid bit

quiz.question: What does the setuid bit on an executable do?
options: Runs the executable with the file owner's privileges instead of the running user's
Makes the file executable by everyone
Sets the file's group to root
quiz.answer: Runs the executable with the file owner's privileges instead of the running user's
quiz.explanation: setuid (chmod u+s) means the executable runs as the file owner (often root). This is how passwd can modify /etc/shadow.

quiz.question: To make a file immutable (cannot be modified even by root), use ___
quiz.explanation: chattr +i sets the immutable attribute. Even root cannot modify, delete, or rename the file until chattr -i removes it.

tracks.name: Process Management
tracks.description: Monitor, control, and manage Linux processes and services.

lessons.title: Process Management: Monitor and Control
lessons.introduction: Every running program is a process. Understanding how to view, monitor, and control processes with ps, top, htop, and kill is fundamental to Linux system administration and debugging.
lessons.purpose: View, monitor, and terminate running processes

sections.title: ps: Process Snapshot
sections.content: ps shows running processes. ps aux shows all processes for all users. ps -ef shows full-format listing. Key columns: PID, %CPU, %MEM, COMMAND.
sections.example: ps aux | grep -E 'apache|nginx' | grep -v grep
sections.explanation: Finds all apache/nginx processes. The 'grep -v grep' excludes the grep command itself from results.

sections.title: top: Live Process Monitor
sections.content: top shows real-time process usage. Press q to quit, M to sort by memory, P to sort by CPU, k to kill a process by PID.
sections.example: top -bn1 | head -20
sections.explanation: -b runs top in batch mode (non-interactive), -n1 takes one snapshot. Useful for scripts and logging.

sections.title: htop: Enhanced Monitor
sections.content: htop is a user-friendly top with color, mouse support, and tree view. Shows process trees, lets you scroll, and has function keys for common operations.
sections.example: htop
sections.explanation: Interactive process monitor. F5 for tree view, F6 to sort, F9 to kill, F10 to quit.

sections.title: Killing Processes
sections.content: kill sends signals to processes. Default is SIGTERM (15) — graceful shutdown. SIGKILL (9) force-kills (cannot be caught). Always try SIGTERM first.
sections.example:
kill 1234          # sends SIGTERM (15)
kill -9 1234       # sends SIGKILL (9) — force kill
kill -HUP 1234     # sends SIGHUP — reload config
killall nginx       # kill all nginx processes by name
sections.explanation: SIGTERM lets the process clean up. SIGKILL is a last resort — the process has no chance to save state.

sections.title: Signals Overview
sections.content: Signals are software interrupts. Key signals: SIGHUP(1) reload, SIGINT(2) interrupt, SIGTERM(15) terminate, SIGKILL(9) force kill, SIGUSR1(10) user-defined.
sections.example:
kill -l       # list all signals
kill -USR1 $(cat /var/run/nginx.pid)   # tell nginx to reopen log files
sections.explanation: Different signals serve different purposes. Many daemons use SIGHUP to reload config without restarting.

sections.title: Process Priority
sections.content: nice values range from -20 (highest priority) to 19 (lowest). renice changes priority of running processes. Higher nice = lower priority.
sections.example:
nice -n 10 ./heavy_task.sh     # run with lower priority
renice -5 -p 1234              # make PID 1234 higher priority
sections.explanation: Use nice for CPU-intensive background tasks. Renice adjusts priority of already-running processes.

common_mistakes: Using kill -9 immediately — always try kill (SIGTERM) first
ps aux | grep process without grep -v grep — the grep itself shows up in results
Confusing PID with PPID — PPID is the parent process ID
Not checking if a process is actually running before trying to kill it
best_practices: Use pgrep to find PIDs: pgrep -f 'pattern' instead of ps aux | grep
Always try SIGTERM before SIGKILL — give processes a chance to clean up
Use htop for interactive monitoring, ps for scripting and snapshots
Monitor with top -bn1 | grep for quick scripted checks

exercises.prompt: Find all processes consuming more than 10% CPU
exercises.hint: Field 3 in ps aux is %CPU. Use awk to filter.

exercises.prompt: Count the total number of running processes
exercises.hint: Count lines of ps aux output (subtract 1 for header)

quiz.question: What is the difference between kill (SIGTERM) and kill -9 (SIGKILL)?
options: SIGTERM is graceful, SIGKILL is forceful and cannot be caught
SIGKILL is graceful, SIGTERM is forceful
SIGTERM requires root, SIGKILL does not
quiz.answer: SIGTERM is graceful, SIGKILL is forceful and cannot be caught
quiz.explanation: SIGTERM lets the process handle the signal and clean up. SIGKILL is handled by the kernel and cannot be caught — the process is killed immediately.

quiz.question: To find a process by name without the grep showing up, use command ___
quiz.explanation: pgrep searches for processes by name or pattern and returns PIDs directly, avoiding the self-matching problem of grep.

lessons.title: Background Jobs & Session Management
lessons.introduction: Running long tasks in the foreground ties up your terminal. Background jobs, nohup, and terminal multiplexers like screen and tmux let you run processes in the background, detach, and reattach — essential for remote server work.
lessons.purpose: Run processes in the background and manage terminal sessions
lessons.syntax: cmd &  |  bg  |  fg  |  jobs  |  nohup cmd  |  screen  |  tmux

sections.title: Backgrounding with &
sections.content: Appending & to a command runs it in the background. The shell returns the PID immediately. The job runs independently of the terminal.
sections.example:
sleep 300 &
# [1] 12345
jobs
sections.explanation: Runs sleep 300 in background. The shell shows the job ID [1] and PID 12345. jobs lists all background jobs.

sections.title: fg and bg
sections.content: fg brings a background job to the foreground. bg sends a stopped job back to the background. Use job IDs (%1, %2) or PIDs.
sections.example:
sleep 300 &
# [1] 12345
fg %1          # bring job 1 to foreground
# Press Ctrl+Z to suspend
bg %1          # resume in background
sections.explanation: Ctrl+Z suspends the current foreground job. bg resumes it in the background. fg brings it back to foreground.

sections.title: nohup: Survive Logout
sections.content: nohup makes a process ignore SIGHUP, so it survives when you log out. Output goes to nohup.out by default.
sections.example: nohup ./backup.sh > backup.log 2>&1 &
sections.explanation: Runs backup.sh in the background, survives logout, stdout/stderr go to backup.log.

sections.title: screen: Virtual Terminals
sections.content: GNU screen creates virtual terminal sessions that persist after disconnect. Create, detach, and reattach sessions.
sections.example:
screen -S mysession     # create named session
# ... work in the screen ...
# Ctrl+A then D to detach
screen -r mysession     # reattach to session
screen -ls              # list all sessions
sections.explanation: Screen sessions survive SSH disconnections. Essential for long-running processes on remote servers.

sections.title: tmux: Modern Multiplexer
sections.content: tmux is a modern alternative to screen with better features. Create sessions, split panes, and manage windows.
sections.example:
tmux new -s work        # create named session
# Ctrl+B then D to detach
tmux attach -t work     # reattach
tmux split-window -h    # split horizontally
tmux list-sessions
sections.explanation: tmux offers panes, windows, and better scripting. The prefix key Ctrl+B is used before all commands.

common_mistakes: Running a process in background with & but not using nohup — it dies on logout
Forgetting to redirect output from background jobs — output clutters the terminal
Not checking jobs before closing a terminal — running processes may be killed
Confusing screen and tmux — they're different tools with similar purposes
best_practices: Use nohup with output redirection for any background process you want to survive logout
Prefer tmux over screen for new setups — it's more modern and feature-rich
Name your sessions: screen -S backup or tmux new -s backup
Use disown to remove a running job from the shell's job table

exercises.prompt: Run sleep 60 in the background and list all background jobs
exercises.hint: Append & to run in background, jobs to list them

exercises.prompt: Start a tmux session named 'monitor', detach from it, and list all tmux sessions
exercises.solution:
tmux new -s monitor
tmux detach
tmux list-sessions
exercises.hint: tmux new -s creates, detach exits without killing, list-sessions shows all

quiz.question: What does nohup do?
options: Makes a process ignore the SIGHUP signal (survives logout)
Runs a process as a daemon
quiz.answer: Makes a process ignore the SIGHUP signal (survives logout)
quiz.explanation: nohup (no hangup) makes a process ignore SIGHUP, which is sent when the terminal disconnects. The process continues running after logout.

quiz.question: To bring a background job to the foreground, use command ___
quiz.explanation: fg brings a background or stopped job to the foreground. Use fg %1 for job 1, or fg PID for a specific process.

lessons.title: systemd: Service Management
lessons.introduction: systemd is the init system and service manager on modern Linux. systemctl controls services, and journalctl manages logs. Understanding systemd is essential for managing daemons, debugging startup issues, and configuring system behavior.
lessons.purpose: Start, stop, enable, and debug system services with systemctl and journalctl

sections.title: systemctl Basics
sections.content: systemctl manages systemd units (services, sockets, mounts, etc.). Start/stop/restart services, check status, enable at boot.
sections.example:
sudo systemctl start nginx
sudo systemctl status nginx
sudo systemctl enable nginx
sudo systemctl stop nginx
sections.explanation: start/stop control the running state. enable/disable controls whether it starts at boot. status shows current state and recent logs.

sections.title: Service Status and Logging
sections.content: systemctl status shows if a service is active, its PID, memory usage, and recent log lines. journalctl -u SERVICE shows full logs.
sections.example:
systemctl status nginx
journalctl -u nginx --since '1 hour ago'
journalctl -u nginx -f
sections.explanation: status gives a quick health check. journalctl -f follows logs in real time (like tail -f for systemd logs).

sections.title: Writing Service Files
sections.content: Custom services are defined in .service files under /etc/systemd/system/. Key sections: [Unit], [Service], [ExecStart].
sections.example:
[Unit]
Description=My Web App
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3 /opt/app/server.py
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
sections.explanation: After= ensures network is up before starting. Restart=always auto-restarts on crash. WantedBy defines the boot target.

sections.title: Reloading systemd
sections.content: After modifying .service files, reload systemd to pick up changes. daemon-reload re-reads unit files without restarting services.
sections.example:
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart myapp
sections.explanation: daemon-reload is required after any .service file change. Then restart the service to apply the new configuration.

sections.title: journalctl: Log Exploration
sections.content: journalctl queries the systemd journal. Filter by unit, time range, priority, or boot. Essential for debugging.
sections.example:
journalctl -u nginx --since '2024-01-01' --until '2024-01-02'
journalctl -p err -b
journalctl --list-boots
sections.explanation: -p err filters by priority (error and above). -b shows only current boot. --list-boots shows all recorded boots.

sections.title: Common Systemd Commands
sections.content: systemctl list-units shows all loaded units. is-active checks if a service is running. is-enabled checks if it starts at boot.
sections.example:
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running
systemctl is-active nginx
systemctl is-enabled nginx
sections.explanation: list-units gives an overview of all services. is-active/is-enabled are useful in scripts to check service state.

common_mistakes: Forgetting systemctl daemon-reload after editing service files
Using service command instead of systemctl — systemctl is the modern standard
Not checking systemctl status after restart — assume nothing, verify everything
Using journalctl without filtering — system journals can be enormous
best_practices: Always check systemctl status after starting/restarting a service
Use journalctl -u SERVICE -f to follow logs when debugging startup failures
Set Restart=always for critical services that should survive crashes
Use systemctl list-units --state=failed to find broken services quickly

exercises.prompt: Check the status of the sshd service and show its last 20 log lines
exercises.hint: systemctl status for quick check, journalctl -u for logs

exercises.prompt: List all failed systemd services on the system
exercises.hint: Use --state=failed to filter only failed units

quiz.question: What must you run after editing a systemd service file?
quiz.explanation: systemctl daemon-reload re-reads all unit files from disk. Without it, systemd uses the cached version and ignores your changes.

quiz.question: To follow nginx logs in real time using journalctl, use flag ___
quiz.explanation: journalctl -u nginx -f follows the journal like tail -f, printing new entries as they arrive.

lessons.title: Process Priority: nice, renice & ionice
lessons.introduction: Not all processes are equal. nice and renice control CPU priority, while ionice controls I/O scheduling. These tools ensure critical processes get resources while background tasks don't starve the system.
lessons.purpose: Control CPU and I/O scheduling priority for processes
lessons.syntax: nice [-n LEVEL] CMD  |  renice [-n] LEVEL [-p PID]  |  ionice [-c CLASS] CMD

sections.title: nice: Launch with Priority
sections.content: nice starts a command with reduced CPU priority. Nice values range from -20 (highest) to 19 (lowest). Default is 0.
sections.example:
nice -n 10 ./heavy_task.sh
nice -n 19 tar czf backup.tar.gz /data/
sections.explanation: Running at nice 10 gives the task lower priority — it yields CPU to important processes

sections.title: renice: Change Running Process Priority
sections.content: renice changes the priority of a running process. Requires appropriate permissions. -p specifies PID.
sections.example:
renice -5 -p 1234
sudo renice -10 -p 1234
renice -n 15 -u username
sections.explanation: Lower nice value = higher priority. Only root can set negative nice values on other users' processes.

sections.title: Understanding Nice Values
sections.content: Nice 0 is normal. Positive values (1-19) are lower priority. Negative values (-1 to -20) are higher priority but require root.
sections.example:
ps -eo pid,ni,comm | head -10
# PID  NI  COMMAND
# 1    0  systemd
# 1234 10  backup.sh
sections.explanation: The NI column shows the nice value. 0 is default, positive means lower priority.

sections.title: ionice: I/O Priority
sections.content: ionice controls disk I/O scheduling classes: real-time (1), best-effort (2), idle (3). Classes 1-2 have priorities 0-7.
sections.example:
ionice -c 3 tar czf archive.tar.gz /data/
ionice -c 2 -n 0 dd if=/dev/sda of=/dev/sdb
ionice -p 1234
sections.explanation: Class 3 (idle) only uses disk when nothing else needs it — perfect for backups

sections.title: Checking Process Priority
sections.content: ps shows priority (PRI) and nice (NI) values. top and htop display them in real time.
sections.example:
ps -eo pid,ni,pri,comm | grep bash
ps -eo pid,ni,pri,comm --sort=-ni | head -10
sections.explanation: Sort by nice value to see which processes have highest/lowest CPU priority

sections.title: Combining nice and ionice
sections.content: For maximum background task flexibility, combine both CPU and I/O priority control.
sections.example:
nice -n 19 ionice -c 3 ./backup.sh
nice -n 15 ionice -c 2 -n 5 ./log_processor.sh
sections.explanation: First: lowest CPU priority AND idle I/O — truly background. Second: low CPU but normal I/O.

common_mistakes: Using negative nice values without root — only root can set nice below 0
Confusing nice value direction — higher number means LOWER priority (counterintuitive)
Not checking ionice class before setting — class 0 means 'no class change', not class 0
best_practices: Use nice -n 19 ionice -c 3 for truly background tasks that shouldn't impact interactive use
Run backups and batch jobs at low priority to preserve system responsiveness
Use ps -eo ni,comm to quickly audit which processes are running at what priority
Set ionice for disk-heavy operations (backups, indexing) to avoid starving interactive I/O

exercises.prompt: Run tar to create a backup at the lowest CPU and I/O priority
exercises.hint: Combine nice -n 19 (lowest CPU) with ionice -c 3 (idle I/O)

exercises.prompt: Find the 5 processes with the lowest nice values (highest priority)
exercises.hint: Use ps -eo with --sort=ni to sort by nice value

quiz.question: What does nice value 19 mean for a process?
quiz.explanation: Nice values range from -20 (highest) to 19 (lowest). 19 is the lowest priority — the process yields CPU to everything else.

quiz.question: To start a command with reduced I/O priority using idle class, use ionice -c ___
quiz.explanation: ionice class 3 is 'idle' — the process only gets disk access when no other process needs it.

tracks.name: Networking Fundamentals
tracks.description: Network diagnostics, remote access, and data transfer tools.

lessons.title: Network Diagnostics: Ping to Packet
lessons.introduction: Network diagnostics are essential for troubleshooting connectivity issues. From simple ping tests to DNS lookups with dig, and HTTP debugging with curl, these tools help you understand and fix network problems.
lessons.purpose: Test connectivity, transfer data, and diagnose network issues
lessons.syntax: ping HOST  |  curl [OPTIONS] URL  |  wget URL  |  ss [OPTIONS]  |  dig DOMAIN

sections.title: ping: Connectivity Test
sections.content: ping sends ICMP echo requests to test if a host is reachable. -c limits the count. Use it as the first step in network troubleshooting.
sections.example:
ping -c 4 google.com
ping -c 4 8.8.8.8
sections.explanation: Sends 4 packets to google.com. Look for response time and packet loss. 0% loss means connectivity is good.

sections.title: curl: HTTP Swiss Army Knife
sections.content: curl transfers data with URLs. -I fetches headers only, -v shows verbose output, -o saves to file, -s suppresses progress.
sections.example:
curl -I https://example.com
curl -s https://api.example.com/data | jq .
curl -o file.zip https://example.com/download.zip
sections.explanation: -I shows only response headers (status code, content type). -s suppresses progress bars for clean output in scripts.

sections.title: wget: File Download
sections.content: wget downloads files from the web. -c resumes interrupted downloads, -q quiet mode, -r recursive for mirroring sites.
sections.example:
wget https://example.com/file.tar.gz
wget -c https://example.com/large.iso
wget -r -np https://example.com/docs/
sections.explanation: -c continues where a previous download left off. -r -np recursively downloads a site without ascending to parent directories.

sections.title: ss: Socket Statistics
sections.content: ss shows network connections, sockets, and statistics. Replaces netstat. -t for TCP, -u for UDP, -l for listening, -n for numeric (no DNS).
sections.example:
ss -tlnp
# State    Recv-Q  Send-Q  Local Address:Port  Process
# LISTEN   0       128     0.0.0.0:22          users:(("sshd",pid=1234))
sections.explanation: Shows all listening TCP ports with the process using them. Essential for checking if a service is actually listening.

sections.title: dig: DNS Lookup
sections.content: dig queries DNS servers for domain information. More detailed than nslookup. Shows A, AAAA, MX, CNAME, and other record types.
sections.example:
dig example.com
 dig +short example.com
 dig MX example.com
sections.explanation: +short gives just the IP address. dig MX shows mail exchange records. Use dig to diagnose DNS resolution issues.

sections.title: ip and ifconfig
sections.content: ip addr shows network interfaces and IPs. ip route shows the routing table. ip is the modern replacement for ifconfig.
sections.example:
ip addr show
ip route show
ip link show eth0
sections.explanation: ip addr shows all interfaces with their IP addresses. ip route shows how traffic is routed. Both are essential for network debugging.

common_mistakes: Using ping without -c — it runs forever until Ctrl+C
Confusing curl and wget — curl is better for APIs/scripts, wget for simple downloads
Using netstat instead of ss — netstat is deprecated on many systems
Not checking DNS before connectivity — dig first, then ping
best_practices: Start network debugging with: ping → dig → curl → ss
Use curl -v to see full request/response headers when debugging APIs
Use ss -tlnp to quickly check if a service is listening on the expected port
Combine dig +short with other commands for scripting DNS lookups

exercises.prompt: Check if port 80 is listening on the local machine
exercises.hint: ss -tlnp shows all listening TCP ports, grep for port 80

exercises.prompt: Fetch the HTTP status code from a URL using curl
exercises.hint: Use curl -w to output just the HTTP response code

quiz.question: Which command shows all listening TCP ports with the owning process?
quiz.explanation: ss -tlnp: -t TCP, -l listening, -n numeric, -p show process. This is the standard way to check listening ports.

quiz.question: To fetch only HTTP response headers with curl, use flag ___
quiz.explanation: curl -I sends a HEAD request, returning only the response headers (status code, content-type, etc.) without the body.

lessons.title: SSH: Secure Remote Access
lessons.introduction: SSH (Secure Shell) is the standard for remote server access, file transfer, and tunneling. Mastering SSH keys, config files, scp, rsync, and port forwarding unlocks secure, efficient remote workflows.
lessons.purpose: Access remote servers, transfer files, and create secure tunnels
lessons.syntax: ssh [USER@]HOST  |  scp SRC DEST  |  rsync -avz SRC DEST  |  ssh -L PORT:HOST:PORT

sections.title: SSH Keys: Passwordless Login
sections.content: SSH keys replace passwords with cryptographic authentication. Generate with ssh-keygen, copy with ssh-copy-id. Keys are stored in ~/.ssh/.
sections.example:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C 'your@email.com'
ssh-copy-id user@server
ssh user@server  # no password needed!
sections.explanation: ed25519 is the recommended key type (fast, secure). ssh-copy-id installs your public key on the remote server.

sections.title: SSH Config File
sections.content: ~/.ssh/config lets you define host aliases and settings. Avoids typing full hostnames and options every time.
sections.example:
Host prod
  HostName 192.168.1.100
  User deploy
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/prod_key
  Port 2222

Host staging
  HostName staging.example.com
  User admin
sections.explanation: Now you can type 'ssh prod' instead of 'ssh -i ~/.ssh/prod_key -p 2222 deploy@192.168.1.100'.

sections.title: scp: Secure Copy
sections.content: scp copies files over SSH. Similar syntax to cp but with a remote path (user@host:path).
sections.example:
scp file.txt user@server:/tmp/
scp user@server:/var/log/nginx.log ./
scp -r ./project/ user@server:/opt/
sections.explanation: Local to remote, remote to local, -r for recursive directory copy. scp uses SSH for encrypted transfer.

sections.title: rsync: Efficient Sync
sections.content: rsync synchronizes files using delta transfer (only sends differences). Much faster than scp for repeated transfers. -a archive, -v verbose, -z compress.
sections.example:
rsync -avz ./project/ user@server:/opt/project/
rsync -avz --delete ./site/ user@server:/var/www/
rsync -avz --exclude='*.log' ./data/ user@server:/backup/
sections.explanation: -a preserves permissions, timestamps, symlinks. --delete removes files on remote that don't exist locally. --exclude filters patterns.

sections.title: SSH Port Forwarding
sections.content: SSH can tunnel traffic: -L for local port forwarding, -R for remote, -D for dynamic (SOCKS proxy).
sections.example:
ssh -L 8080:localhost:80 user@server
ssh -D 1080 user@server
ssh -R 9090:localhost:3000 user@server
sections.explanation: -L: access remote port 80 via local port 8080. -D: create a SOCKS proxy on port 1080. -R: expose local port 3000 to remote port 9090.

sections.title: SSH Agent
sections.content: ssh-agent caches your decrypted private key so you don't enter the passphrase repeatedly. eval ssh-agent and ssh-add to start.
sections.example:
eval $(ssh-agent -s)
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
ssh-add -l  # list loaded keys
sections.explanation: ssh-agent runs in background, holds decrypted keys. ssh-add loads keys into the agent. Keys stay loaded until agent stops.

common_mistakes: Using scp when rsync would be faster — rsync only transfers changed parts
Forgetting to set correct permissions on ~/.ssh (700) and keys (600)
Not using ssh-copy-id — manually copying keys often gets permissions wrong
Hardcoding passwords in scripts instead of using SSH keys
best_practices: Use ed25519 keys (ssh-keygen -t ed25519) — faster and more secure than RSA
Set up ~/.ssh/config for frequently accessed servers
Use rsync --delete carefully — it makes the destination mirror the source exactly
Use ssh-agent to avoid re-entering key passphrases

exercises.prompt: Generate an SSH key pair and copy the public key to a remote server
exercises.hint: ssh-keygen to create, ssh-copy-id to install on remote

exercises.prompt: Sync a local directory to a remote server using rsync, excluding .git directories
exercises.hint: Use rsync -avz with --exclude for patterns to skip

quiz.question: Why is rsync generally preferred over scp for repeated file transfers?
options: rsync encrypts data, scp does not
rsync transfers only changed portions of files (delta transfer)
rsync is always faster for single files
quiz.answer: rsync transfers only changed portions of files (delta transfer)
quiz.explanation: rsync uses a delta algorithm to identify and transfer only the changed parts of files, making repeated syncs much faster than scp's full transfer.

quiz.question: To generate an ed25519 SSH key pair, use ssh-keygen with flag ___
quiz.explanation: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 creates a modern, fast, secure key pair. Ed25519 is preferred over RSA for new keys.

lessons.title: curl: HTTP Mastery
lessons.introduction: curl is the Swiss Army knife of HTTP. From simple downloads to complex API interactions with authentication, headers, cookies, and proxies — mastering curl is essential for debugging web services, testing APIs, and automating HTTP workflows.
lessons.purpose: Interact with HTTP APIs, handle authentication, and debug web services

sections.title: Basic HTTP Methods
sections.content: curl supports GET (default), POST (-X POST), PUT, DELETE, and PATCH. -d sends data, -H sets headers.
sections.example:
curl https://api.example.com/users
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"name":"Alice"}'
sections.explanation: GET retrieves data, POST creates data. -H sets the content type for JSON API calls.

sections.title: Headers and Cookies
sections.content: Use -H to set custom headers. -b sends cookies, -c saves cookies. Essential for authenticated sessions.
sections.example:
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer TOKEN' https://api.example.com/me
curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt https://example.com/login
sections.explanation: Authorization header for token auth. -b/-c for cookie-based session management.

sections.title: Authentication Methods
sections.content: curl supports basic (-u), digest, bearer token, and client certificate authentication.
sections.example:
curl -u user:password https://api.example.com/admin
curl --cert client.pem --key client-key.pem https://secure.api.com
sections.explanation: -u sends HTTP Basic auth. --cert/--key for client certificate (mTLS) authentication.

sections.title: Response Handling
sections.content: -o saves to file, -O uses remote filename, -s suppresses progress, -S shows errors, -w custom output format.
sections.example:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}s' https://example.com
curl -sS https://api.example.com/data | jq .
sections.explanation: -w with format specifiers for metrics. -sS suppresses progress but shows errors.

sections.title: Proxy Support
sections.content: curl supports HTTP, HTTPS, and SOCKS proxies via -x or environment variables.
sections.example:
curl -x http://proxy.example.com:8080 https://target.com
curl -x socks5://localhost:1080 https://target.com
export https_proxy=http://proxy:8080
sections.explanation: Use -x for one-off proxy connections, or set environment variables for persistent proxy usage.

sections.title: Advanced Options
sections.content: -L follows redirects, -k skips SSL verification (testing only), --connect-timeout limits connection time, - retry retries failed requests.
sections.example:
curl -L -k https://example.com/redirect
curl --connect-timeout 5 --retry 3 https://unreliable.api.com
sections.explanation: -L is essential for URLs that redirect. --retry handles transient network failures gracefully.

common_mistakes: Forgetting -L for URLs that redirect — curl won't follow redirects without it
Using -k in production — it disables SSL verification, a security risk
Not quoting JSON data in -d — shell interprets special characters without quotes
Confusing -d (POST data) with -G (convert to GET with data as query params)
best_practices: Use -sS -o /dev/null -w for scripted HTTP health checks with just status code and timing
Always quote JSON in -d: -d '{"key":"value"}' — the shell will eat unquoted braces
Use curl --connect-timeout for scripts that shouldn't hang on unreachable hosts
Store API tokens in environment variables, not in scripts: -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

exercises.prompt: Send a POST request to http://httpbin.org/post with JSON body {"test": true} and show the response
exercises.solution: curl -s -X POST http://httpbin.org/post -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"test": true}' | jq .
exercises.hint: Use curl -X POST with -H for content type and -d for the JSON body

exercises.prompt: Check the HTTP status code and total time for https://example.com
exercises.hint: Use curl -w with %{http_code} and %{time_total} format specifiers

quiz.question: What does curl -L do?
options: Follows HTTP redirects to the final destination
quiz.answer: Follows HTTP redirects to the final destination
quiz.explanation: -L (location) follows HTTP 3xx redirects. Without it, curl returns the redirect response instead of the final content.

quiz.question: To send HTTP Basic authentication with curl, use flag ___
quiz.explanation: curl -u user:password sends HTTP Basic Authorization header. Format: -u username:password.

tracks.name: Git & Version Control
tracks.description: Master Git fundamentals and branching strategies for effective version control.

lessons.title: Git Fundamentals: Track Everything
lessons.introduction: Git is the world's most popular version control system. It tracks every change to your code, lets you collaborate safely, and provides a complete history of your project. Mastering git init, add, commit, status, log, and diff is the foundation.
lessons.purpose: Initialize repos, stage changes, commit snapshots, and inspect history
lessons.syntax: git init  |  git add FILE  |  git commit -m 'msg'  |  git status  |  git log  |  git diff

sections.title: git init: Starting a Repository
sections.content: git init creates a new Git repository. It creates a .git directory that stores all version history. git clone copies an existing repository.
sections.example:
git init myproject
cd myproject
git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git
sections.explanation: init creates a fresh repo. clone downloads an existing one with full history. Both create a working directory with version tracking.

sections.title: git add: Staging Changes
sections.content: git add moves changes from the working directory to the staging area. Only staged changes are included in the next commit. Use . for all files.
sections.example:
git add server.log
git add '*.csv'
git add -p  # stage interactively, hunk by hunk
git add .   # stage everything
sections.explanation: The staging area lets you craft commits by selecting exactly which changes to include. git add -p is powerful for splitting changes.

sections.title: git commit: Saving Snapshots
sections.content: git commit saves staged changes with a message. The -m flag provides the message inline. Commits are immutable snapshots in history.
sections.example:
git commit -m 'Add error analysis pipeline'
git commit -am 'Fix parsing bug'  # add + commit tracked files
sections.explanation: -am combines add and commit for already-tracked files. Always write clear, concise commit messages explaining the 'why'.

sections.title: git status: Check State
sections.content: git status shows the current state: modified files, staged changes, untracked files, and which branch you're on.
sections.example:
git status
# On branch main
# Changes to be committed: new file: employees.csv
# Changes not staged: modified: server.log
sections.explanation: Run git status frequently — it tells you exactly what will happen in the next commit.

sections.title: git log: View History
sections.content: git log shows commit history. --oneline for compact view, --graph for branch visualization, --stat for file changes per commit.
sections.example:
git log --oneline -10
git log --graph --oneline --all
git log --stat -5
sections.explanation: --oneline shows one line per commit. --graph shows branch/merge structure. --stat adds file change stats.

sections.title: git diff: See Changes
sections.content: git diff shows unstaged changes. git diff --staged shows staged changes. git diff HEAD shows all changes since last commit.
sections.example:
git diff server.log
git diff --staged
git diff HEAD~3..HEAD  # changes in last 3 commits
sections.explanation: Use diff before committing to review exactly what changed. diff HEAD compares working directory to last commit.

common_mistakes: Committing without checking git status first — you might include unwanted files
Using git add . before checking what's modified — could add secrets or temp files
Writing vague commit messages like 'fix' or 'update' — future you won't understand
Not using .gitignore — ends up tracking node_modules, .env, etc.
best_practices: Run git status before every commit to verify what you're saving
Write commit messages that explain WHY, not just what changed
Use git add -p to stage specific hunks for cleaner commits
Create a .gitignore early to exclude build artifacts and secrets

exercises.prompt: Initialize a new git repository, add a file, and make your first commit
exercises.solution:
git init
echo 'hello' > README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m 'Initial commit: add README'
exercises.hint: git init → git add → git commit

exercises.prompt: Show the last 5 commits in compact one-line format
exercises.hint: Use --oneline for compact output, -5 to limit

quiz.question: What is the difference between git add and git commit?
options: git add stages changes, git commit saves staged changes as a snapshot
git commit stages changes, git add saves them
git add saves to remote, git commit saves locally
quiz.answer: git add stages changes, git commit saves staged changes as a snapshot
quiz.explanation: The staging area (index) is an intermediate step. git add prepares changes, git commit records them permanently in history.

quiz.question: To see only the file change stats in the last 3 commits, use git log with flag ___
quiz.explanation: git log --stat shows each commit with the files changed and lines added/removed. Combined with -3 for last 3 commits.

lessons.title: Git Branching: Parallel Development
lessons.introduction: Branching is Git's superpower. It lets multiple developers work on different features simultaneously without interfering with each other. Understanding branch, checkout, merge, rebase, and stash is essential for team development.
lessons.purpose: Create branches, merge changes, and manage parallel development workflows
lessons.syntax: git branch NAME  |  git checkout -b NAME  |  git merge BRANCH  |  git rebase BRANCH  |  git stash

sections.title: Creating and Switching Branches
sections.content: git branch creates a branch. git checkout -b creates and switches in one step. git switch is the modern alternative to checkout for switching.
sections.example:
git branch feature-login
git checkout -b feature-api
git switch main
sections.explanation: checkout -b is the most common workflow: create a new branch and immediately start working on it.

sections.title: Merging Branches
sections.content: git merge combines a branch into the current branch. Fast-forward merges are linear. Three-way merges create a merge commit when branches diverged.
sections.example:
git checkout main
git merge feature-login
# Merge made by 'ort' strategy.
#  3 files changed, 45 insertions(+), 12 deletions(-)
sections.explanation: Always merge INTO the target branch. Switch to main, then merge feature. Git automatically combines the changes.

sections.title: Rebasing
sections.content: git rebase replays commits from one branch onto another, creating a linear history. Interactive rebase (-i) lets you rewrite, squash, and reorder commits.
sections.example:
git checkout feature-api
git rebase main
git rebase -i HEAD~3  # interactive: last 3 commits
sections.explanation: Rebase makes history linear and clean. Interactive rebase lets you 'squash' multiple commits into one, edit messages, or reorder.

sections.title: Resolving Merge Conflicts
sections.content: When Git can't auto-merge, it marks conflicts with <<<<<<< HEAD. Edit the file to resolve, then git add and git commit.
sections.example:
# <<<<<<< HEAD
# current change
# =======
# incoming change
# >>>>>>> feature
# After resolving:
git add resolved_file.txt
git commit
sections.explanation: Conflict markers show both versions. Choose the correct code (or combine both), remove the markers, stage, and commit.

sections.title: git stash: Temporary Save
sections.content: git stash saves uncommitted changes temporarily. Perfect for switching branches quickly. stash pop restores, stash list shows all.
sections.example:
git stash                    # save current changes
git checkout main            # switch to main
git pull                     # update
git checkout feature          # switch back
git stash pop                # restore changes
sections.explanation: Stash is like a clipboard for changes. stash pop applies and removes. stash apply applies but keeps the stash.

sections.title: Branch Management
sections.content: git branch lists branches. -d deletes merged branches. -D force-deletes. git branch -a shows all including remote tracking branches.
sections.example:
git branch
git branch -a
git branch -d feature-login
git push origin --delete feature-login
sections.explanation: Clean up merged branches regularly. -a shows remote branches too. Delete both local and remote when done.

common_mistakes: Merging into the wrong branch — always switch to the TARGET first
Rebasing shared/public branches — rebase rewrites history, which breaks collaborators
Not resolving all conflict markers before committing
Accidentally deleting unmerged branches — use -d (safe) not -D (force)
best_practices: Use descriptive branch names: feature/user-auth, fix/login-bug, docs/api-guide
Merge or rebase regularly to avoid large divergences
Delete branches after merging to keep the repo clean
Use git stash when you need to quickly switch contexts

exercises.prompt: Create a new branch called 'feature-report', switch to it, make a commit, then switch back to main
exercises.solution:
git checkout -b feature-report
echo 'report code' > report.sh
git add report.sh
git commit -m 'Add report script'
git switch main
exercises.hint: git checkout -b creates and switches, commit, then git switch main

exercises.prompt: Stash current changes, pull latest from main, then restore your stashed changes
exercises.solution:
git stash
git pull origin main
git stash pop
exercises.hint: stash saves, pull updates, stash pop restores

quiz.question: What is the key difference between git merge and git rebase?
options: Merge creates a merge commit; rebase replays commits for linear history
Rebase is for undoing changes, merge is for applying them
Merge only works locally, rebase works with remote
quiz.answer: Merge creates a merge commit; rebase replays commits for linear history
quiz.explanation: Merge preserves the branch history with a merge commit. Rebase rewrites commits to appear as if they were made on top of the target branch, creating linear history.

quiz.question: To save uncommitted changes temporarily, use git ___
quiz.explanation: git stash saves your working directory and staging area changes. Use stash pop or stash apply to restore them later.

lessons.title: Git Advanced: bisect, cherry-pick & reflog
lessons.introduction: Beyond branches and merges, Git offers powerful tools for debugging with bisect, selectively applying commits with cherry-pick, recovering lost work with reflog, and managing complex projects with worktrees and submodules.
lessons.purpose: Debug with bisect, selectively apply commits, recover lost work, and manage complex repos
lessons.syntax: git bisect  |  git cherry-pick  |  git reflog  |  git worktree  |  git submodule

sections.title: git bisect: Binary Search for Bugs
sections.content: bisect performs a binary search through commit history to find the exact commit that introduced a bug. Mark commits as good/bad and Git narrows down the culprit.
sections.example:
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD
git bisect good v1.0
# Git checks out a middle commit — test it
git bisect good  # or git bisect bad
git bisect reset
sections.explanation: Automatically finds the bug-introducing commit in O(log n) time — even across thousands of commits

sections.title: git cherry-pick: Selective Commit Application
sections.content: cherry-pick applies a specific commit from any branch to your current branch. Useful for backporting fixes or applying individual changes.
sections.example:
git cherry-pick abc1234
git cherry-pick abc1234..def5678
git cherry-pick --no-commit abc1234
sections.explanation: Apply one commit, a range, or stage changes without committing — surgical precision

sections.title: git reflog: Recovery Vault
sections.content: reflog records every HEAD movement, including lost commits, force pushes, and rebases. It's your safety net for recovering from mistakes.
sections.explanation: Every action is logged. You can recover deleted branches, lost commits, and undo resets.

sections.title: git worktree: Multiple Working Trees
sections.content: worktree lets you check out multiple branches simultaneously in separate directories. No need to stash or switch branches.
sections.example:
git worktree add ../hotfix-branch hotfix
git worktree list
git worktree remove ../hotfix-branch
sections.explanation: Work on a hotfix while keeping your feature branch intact — parallel development without stashing

sections.title: git submodule: Project Dependencies
sections.content: submodule embeds one Git repository inside another. Useful for managing dependencies and shared libraries.
sections.example:
git submodule add https://github.com/user/lib.git libs/lib
git submodule update --init --recursive
git submodule foreach git pull
sections.explanation: Adds external repos as subdirectories. update --init clones them. foreach runs commands in each.

sections.title: git blame: Line History
sections.content: blame shows who last modified each line of a file and when. -L limits to specific line ranges.
sections.example:
git blame server.log
git blame -L 10,20 server.log
git blame -e server.log
sections.explanation: -L limits to lines 10-20. -e shows email instead of name. Great for understanding code ownership.

common_mistakes: Using cherry-pick on merge commits — it replays only one parent, which may cause conflicts
Forgetting git bisect reset — you're stuck in bisect mode until you reset
Adding submodules without --recursive — nested submodules won't be cloned
Not checking reflog after a force push — lost commits are still there in reflog
best_practices: Use git bisect with a test script: git bisect run ./test.sh for fully automated bisection
Use cherry-pick --no-commit when you want to review changes before committing
Check reflog immediately after accidental resets — it's your safety net
Prefer git worktree over stash for context switches that may take a while

exercises.prompt: Use git bisect to find which commit introduced a bug, testing with a script
exercises.solution:
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD
git bisect good v1.0
git bisect run ./test_script.sh
git bisect reset
exercises.hint: bisect run automates the binary search with a test script

exercises.prompt: Recover a deleted branch using git reflog
exercises.hint: reflog shows all HEAD movements — find the last commit on the deleted branch

quiz.question: What does git bisect do?
options: Binary searches commit history to find which commit introduced a bug
Merges two branches by selecting the best parts of each
Creates a bisected copy of the repository
quiz.answer: Binary searches commit history to find which commit introduced a bug
quiz.explanation: git bisect uses binary search: mark good/bad commits and it automatically finds the exact commit that introduced the bug.

quiz.question: To recover lost commits after a reset, use git ___
quiz.explanation: git reflog records every HEAD movement. Lost commits from resets, rebases, or force pushes are still accessible through reflog.

tracks.name: User & System Administration
tracks.description: Manage users, groups, scheduled tasks, and system services.

lessons.title: User & Group Management
lessons.introduction: Linux is a multi-user system. Managing users and groups — creating accounts, setting passwords, assigning groups, and configuring sudo access — is fundamental to system security and administration.
lessons.purpose: Create, modify, and manage user accounts, groups, and sudo access
lessons.syntax: useradd [OPTIONS] USER  |  usermod [OPTIONS] USER  |  passwd USER  |  groupadd GROUP

sections.title: useradd: Creating Users
sections.content: useradd creates a new user account. -m creates a home directory, -s sets the shell, -G adds supplementary groups.
sections.example:
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G sudo developer
cat /etc/passwd | grep developer
sections.explanation: -m creates /home/developer. -s /bin/bash gives a usable shell. -G sudo grants sudo group membership.

sections.title: passwd: Setting Passwords
sections.content: passwd sets or changes a user's password. Running as root, you can set any user's password. Regular users can only change their own.
sections.example:
sudo passwd developer
echo 'developer:password123' | sudo chpasswd
sections.explanation: passwd prompts interactively. chpasswd accepts username:password pairs — useful for scripted user creation.

sections.title: usermod: Modifying Users
sections.content: usermod changes existing user properties. -aG appends to groups (without -a, it REPLACES), -L locks, -U unlocks, -d changes home dir.
sections.example:
sudo usermod -aG docker developer
sudo usermod -s /bin/zsh developer
sudo usermod -L developer  # lock account
sections.explanation: -aG is critical: without -a, usermod REPLACES all groups. Always use -aG to append to supplementary groups.

sections.title: Groups and /etc/group
sections.content: Groups organize users. /etc/group defines groups and their members. useradd -G adds supplementary groups. newgrp switches effective group.
sections.example:
cat /etc/group | grep developers
groupadd developers
sudo usermod -aG developers alice
ewgrp developers
sections.explanation: Each user has a primary group (in /etc/passwd) and supplementary groups (in /etc/group). newgrp changes your active group.

sections.title: sudo Configuration
sections.content: /etc/sudoers defines who can run what as root. Use visudo to edit safely (syntax checks). Or add users to the sudo group.
sections.example:
sudo visudo
# Or add to sudo group:
sudo usermod -aG sudo developer
# Then user can run:
sudo apt update
sections.explanation: visudo validates syntax before saving — prevents locking yourself out. The sudo group typically has full root access.

sections.title: User Information Commands
sections.content: whoami shows current user. id shows UID, GID, and groups. who shows logged-in users. last shows login history.
sections.example:
whoami
id developer
id -nG developer  # just group names
who
last -5 developer
sections.explanation: id is the most useful — shows all group memberships. -nG gives just group names for scripting.

common_mistakes: Using usermod -G (replaces ALL groups) instead of -aG (appends) — users lose existing groups
Not using visudo to edit /etc/sudoers — a syntax error can lock you out of root
Setting weak passwords — always use strong, unique passwords
Forgetting to set a shell — useradd without -s gives /bin/sh by default
best_practices: Use -m with useradd to always create a home directory
Always use -aG to append groups, never bare -G unless you intend to replace
Use visudo for sudoers edits — it validates syntax before saving
Document user accounts and their purposes in a team wiki

exercises.prompt: Create a new user 'deploy' with a home directory and bash shell
exercises.hint: -m creates home dir, -s sets the login shell

exercises.prompt: Show all groups that the user 'developer' belongs to
exercises.hint: id -nG shows group names only

quiz.question: What happens if you use usermod -G instead of -aG?
options: It appends the user to the new group
It replaces ALL supplementary groups with just the new one
It removes the user from all groups
quiz.answer: It replaces ALL supplementary groups with just the new one
quiz.explanation: -G (without -a) replaces all supplementary groups. -aG appends to existing groups. Always use -aG unless you intentionally want to replace.

quiz.question: The safe way to edit /etc/sudoers is with command ___
quiz.explanation: visudo checks syntax before saving, preventing a typo from locking you out of root access.

lessons.title: Scheduled Tasks & Service Management
lessons.introduction: Automation is the backbone of system administration. Cron handles recurring tasks, at handles one-time scheduling, and logrotate manages log file rotation. Together they keep systems running smoothly without manual intervention.
lessons.purpose: Schedule recurring and one-time tasks, manage log rotation
lessons.syntax: crontab -e  |  at TIME  |  systemctl [OPTIONS]  |  logrotate CONFIG

sections.title: crontab: Recurring Tasks
sections.content: crontab defines scheduled tasks. Fields: minute, hour, day, month, weekday, command. crontab -e edits, crontab -l lists.
sections.example:
# Run backup every day at 2 AM
0 2 * * * /opt/scripts/backup.sh
# Run cleanup every Sunday at midnight
0 0 * * 0 /opt/scripts/cleanup.sh
# Check disk space every 5 minutes
*/5 * * * * /opt/scripts/check_disk.sh
sections.explanation: * means 'every'. */5 means 'every 5 units'. 0 2 * * * = minute 0, hour 2, every day/month/weekday.

sections.title: Crontab Special Strings
sections.content: Cron supports shorthand: @reboot (at startup), @daily, @weekly, @monthly. These replace the time fields.
sections.explanation: @reboot runs once at system startup. @daily = 0 0 * * *. @weekly = 0 0 * * 0. @monthly = 0 0 1 * *.

sections.title: at: One-Time Scheduling
sections.content: at schedules a single task for a specific time. Enter commands, end with Ctrl+D. atq lists, atrm removes.
sections.example:
echo '/opt/scripts/report.sh' | at 3pm tomorrow
atq
atrm 3
sections.explanation: at is for one-off tasks. 'at 3pm tomorrow' runs once. atq shows the queue, atrm removes a job by number.

sections.title: Logrotate: Log Management
sections.content: logrotate rotates, compresses, and manages log files. Config files in /etc/logrotate.d/. Handles daily/weekly rotation, compression, and retention.
sections.example:
# /etc/logrotate.d/myapp
/var/log/myapp/*.log {
  daily
  rotate 7
  compress
  missingok
  notifempty
  create 644 www-data www-data
}
sections.explanation: Rotates daily, keeps 7 days, compresses old logs, creates new log with proper permissions. missingok and notifempty handle edge cases.

sections.title: systemctl for System Services
sections.content: systemctl manages systemd services. start/stop/restart for runtime, enable/disable for boot behavior. list-units shows all services.
sections.example:
sudo systemctl restart nginx
sudo systemctl enable nginx
systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running
sections.explanation: enable creates symlinks so the service starts at boot. start only starts it for the current session.

sections.title: Anacron: For Non-24/7 Systems
sections.content: anacron runs periodic jobs on systems that aren't always on (laptops). Unlike cron, it catches up on missed runs. Config in /etc/anacrontab.
sections.explanation: If a laptop was off during a cron job's scheduled time, anacron runs it when the system comes back. Used for daily/weekly maintenance on desktops.
sections.example:
cat /etc/anacrontab
# period  delay  job-id     command
1         5      daily      test -x /usr/sbin/anacron && /usr/sbin/anacron -s

common_mistakes: Cron jobs don't inherit your PATH — use full paths to commands
Forgetting to redirect cron output — uncaught errors send email to root
Using at without checking if the job ran — always verify with atq
Not testing logrotate configs — use logrotate -d for debug/dry-run
best_practices: Always redirect cron output: script.sh >> /var/log/script.log 2>&1
Use full paths in cron (e.g., /usr/bin/python3 not python3)
Test logrotate configs with logrotate -d (dry-run) before deploying
Log important cron job starts/completions for debugging

exercises.prompt: Create a cron job that runs a backup script every day at midnight
exercises.hint: 0 0 * * * = every day at midnight. Use crontab - to pipe in the entry.

exercises.prompt: Schedule a one-time task to run a report script at 5 PM today
exercises.hint: Use at with a time specification, pipe the command to it

quiz.question: What does the cron expression '*/15 * * * *' do?
quiz.explanation: */15 in the minute field means 'every 15 minutes'. The five fields are: minute, hour, day, month, weekday.

quiz.question: To see all cron jobs for the current user, use crontab with flag ___
quiz.explanation: crontab -l lists (prints) the current user's crontab entries. crontab -e edits them.

lessons.title: Backup & Restore: Data Protection
lessons.introduction: Data loss is catastrophic. Mastering tar, rsync, and dd for backups — including incremental strategies — ensures you can recover from hardware failures, accidental deletions, and disasters. Every sysadmin needs these skills.
lessons.purpose: Create full, incremental, and differential backups; restore data from various sources
lessons.syntax: tar [OPTIONS]  |  rsync [OPTIONS] SRC DEST  |  dd if=SRC of=DEST

sections.title: tar: Archive and Compress
sections.content: tar creates archives. -c create, -x extract, -z gzip, -j bzip2, -f filename. -v verbose, -C change directory.
sections.example:
tar -czf backup.tar.gz /data/
tar -xzf backup.tar.gz -C /restore/
tar -cjf backup.tar.bz2 /data/
sections.explanation: -czf creates a gzipped archive. -xzf extracts it. -C specifies the target directory.

sections.title: tar with Exclusions
sections.content: Use --exclude to skip files/directories. --exclude-from reads patterns from a file. Essential for clean backups.
sections.example:
tar -czf backup.tar.gz --exclude='*.log' --exclude='.git' /project/
tar -czf data.tar.gz --exclude-from=exclude-list.txt /data/
sections.explanation: Excludes log files and git history from the archive — keeps backups clean and small.

sections.title: rsync: Incremental Sync
sections.content: rsync transfers only changed files using delta algorithm. -a archive mode, -v verbose, -z compress, --delete mirrors source.
sections.example:
rsync -avz /data/ user@backup:/backup/data/
rsync -avz --delete /data/ user@backup:/backup/data/
rsync -avz --exclude='*.tmp' /data/ /backup/
sections.explanation: rsync is ideal for incremental backups — only changed data is transferred. --delete makes destination mirror source.

sections.title: rsync with SSH
sections.content: rsync uses SSH by default for remote transfers. -e ssh for custom SSH options. -P shows progress and allows resume.
sections.example:
rsync -avzP -e 'ssh -p 2222' /data/ user@server:/backup/
rsync -avz --bwlimit=1000 /data/ user@server:/backup/
sections.explanation: -e ssh for custom SSH. --bwlimit throttles transfer speed to avoid saturating the network.

sections.title: dd: Block-Level Backup
sections.content: dd copies at the block level — useful for disk images, partition backups, and bootable USB creation.
sections.example:
dd if=/dev/sda of=/backup/disk.img bs=4M status=progress
dd if=/backup/disk.img of=/dev/sdb bs=4M status=progress
sections.explanation: Creates an exact copy of a disk. Use for full disk backups or cloning. bs=4M for speed.

sections.title: Incremental Backup Strategy
sections.content: tar supports incremental backups with --listed-incremental. First full, then only changes since last backup.
sections.example:
# Full backup
tar -czf full.tar.gz --listed-incremental=/tmp/snap.snar /data/
# Incremental (only changes)
tar -czf incr.tar.gz --listed-incremental=/tmp/snap.snar /data/
# Restore full first, then incrementals in order
sections.explanation: --listed-incremental tracks file changes. The snapshot file records what changed since the last backup.

common_mistakes: Using dd without bs= — default 512-byte blocks are extremely slow for large disks
Forgetting trailing slashes in rsync: /data/ vs /data makes a big difference
Not testing restore procedures — a backup you can't restore is useless
Running dd on the wrong device — dd has no confirmation prompt, it overwrites immediately
best_practices: Always test backups by doing a test restore to a separate location
Use rsync --delete carefully — it makes destination an exact mirror of source
Follow the 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 different media, 1 offsite
Use --dry-run with rsync first to preview what will be transferred

exercises.prompt: Create a compressed backup of the current directory excluding .git and *.log files
exercises.hint: Use tar -czf with --exclude for patterns to skip

exercises.prompt: Use rsync to sync the current directory to /backup/ with compression and dry-run first
exercises.hint: Use --dry-run to preview changes before actually syncing

quiz.question: What is the key difference between tar and rsync for backups?
options: tar is faster, rsync is slower
tar creates a single archive file, rsync syncs directories preserving structure
rsync can only work locally, tar works remotely
quiz.answer: tar creates a single archive file, rsync syncs directories preserving structure
quiz.explanation: tar bundles files into a single archive. rsync synchronizes directories, transferring only changed files — ideal for incremental backups.

quiz.question: To preview what rsync will transfer without actually doing it, use flag ___
quiz.explanation: --dry-run (or -n) shows what would be transferred without making changes. Essential for verifying rsync behavior.

tracks.name: Advanced Text Processing
tracks.description: Master advanced sed, awk, and file comparison tools for complex text transformations.

lessons.title: Advanced sed: Hold Space & Branching
lessons.introduction: sed's true power lies beyond simple substitution. The hold space, branching commands (b, t), and multi-line processing let you perform complex text transformations that would otherwise require a full programming language.
lessons.purpose: Perform complex text transformations using sed's advanced features

sections.title: The Hold Space
sections.content: sed maintains two buffers: the pattern space (current line) and the hold space (storage area). Commands: h (copy pattern to hold), H (append), g (copy hold to pattern), G (append).
sections.example: sed -n 'h;n;H;g;p' server.log
sections.explanation: Copies line 1 to hold, gets line 2, appends to hold, copies hold to pattern, prints. Result: pairs of lines printed together.

sections.title: Branching: b and t
sections.content: b=label jumps to a label. t=label jumps if the last substitution succeeded. These enable conditional logic and loops in sed.
sections.example: sed -E ':loop; s/([0-9]+) ([0-9]+)/\2 \1/; t loop' file.txt
sections.explanation: Repeatedly swaps pairs of numbers until no more swaps occur. The t command checks if s/// succeeded.

sections.title: Multi-Line Processing
sections.content: N joins the next line into the pattern space. P prints up to the first newline. D deletes up to the first newline. These enable line-pair operations.
sections.example: sed 'N; s/\n/ /' file.txt
sections.explanation: Joins every pair of lines into one line by replacing the newline between them.

sections.title: Delete Patterns
sections.content: Use sed ranges and commands for complex deletion patterns. Delete blank lines, ranges between markers, or nth occurrences.
sections.example:
sed '/^$/d' file.txt                    # remove blank lines
sed '/START/,/END/d' file.txt            # remove between markers
sed '0~2d' file.txt                     # remove every other line
sections.explanation: 0~2d deletes lines 2, 4, 6, ... (every second line starting from 2). The range syntax handles marker-based deletion.

sections.title: Insert and Append
sections.content: i\ inserts text before the current line. a\ appends after. c\ replaces the entire line.
sections.example:
sed '3i\New line inserted here' file.txt
sed '/ERROR/a\--- FOLLOWUP LOG ---' server.log
sed 's/^WARNING/CRITICAL/' file.txt
sections.explanation: i and a are useful for adding headers, separators, or context lines. s/// with no /g replaces the first match.

sections.title: Real-World sed Pipeline
sections.content: Combining sed with other tools creates powerful transformations. Remove headers, transform formats, and extract structured data.
sections.example: sed '1d; s/,/	/g; s/"//g' employees.csv | awk -F'\t' '{print $2, $4}'
sections.explanation: Removes CSV header, replaces commas with tabs, strips quotes, then awk extracts name and salary columns.

common_mistakes: Confusing pattern space and hold space — pattern space holds the current line, hold space is storage
Using single vs double quotes around sed scripts — double quotes let shell expand $variables
Not using -n with commands that need explicit p — without it, pattern space is auto-printed
Forgetting that g replaces the pattern space (losing the original line) vs G which appends
best_practices: Test multi-line sed on small files first — debugging is harder than single-line
Use labels and branching sparingly — if logic gets complex, switch to awk
Use sed -n with p to control exactly what gets printed
Pipe to cat -A to see hidden characters when debugging sed output

exercises.prompt: Remove all blank lines from server.log using sed
exercises.hint: ^$ matches empty lines, d deletes them

exercises.prompt: Swap every pair of lines in a file (line 1 with 2, 3 with 4, etc.)
exercises.hint: Use N to join next line, then rearrange the content

quiz.question: What does the 'h' command do in sed?
options: Copies the pattern space to the hold space
quiz.answer: Copies the pattern space to the hold space
quiz.explanation: h copies (overwrites) the hold space with the pattern space. H appends. g copies hold to pattern. G appends hold to pattern.

quiz.question: In sed, to join the next line into the pattern space, use command ___
quiz.explanation: N reads the next line and appends it to the pattern space with a newline separator. Used for multi-line operations.

lessons.title: Advanced awk: Beyond the Basics
lessons.introduction: awk is a complete programming language for text processing. Advanced features like BEGIN/END blocks, printf formatting, getline for multi-file processing, and user-defined functions make it capable of complex data analysis pipelines.
lessons.purpose: Build sophisticated text processing programs with awk

sections.title: BEGIN and END Blocks
sections.content: BEGIN runs before processing any input. END runs after all input. The main pattern/action runs for each line. Together they form a complete program structure.
sections.example: awk 'BEGIN {print "=== Report ==="; total=0} {total+=$4} END {print "Total:", total}' employees.csv
sections.explanation: Prints a header before processing, sums the salary column, prints total after all lines are processed.

sections.title: printf: Formatted Output
sections.content: printf formats output like C's printf. %s string, %d integer, %f float, %-20s left-aligned 20-char string, %05d zero-padded.
sections.example: awk -F',' 'NR>1 {printf "%-20s %10s %8.2f\n", $2, $3, $4}' employees.csv
sections.explanation: Left-aligns name in 20 chars, right-aligns department in 10, formats salary as 8-char float with 2 decimals.

sections.title: getline: Reading Multiple Sources
sections.content: getline reads the next line. getline < file reads from a file. 'cmd | getline' reads from a command's output. Each getline call advances the input.
sections.example: awk '{getline line < "config.txt"; print $0, line}' data.txt
sections.explanation: For each line in data.txt, reads the next line from config.txt. Useful for processing paired files.

sections.title: User-Defined Functions
sections.content: awk supports functions with local variables. Define with function name(args) { local var; ... return value }.
sections.explanation: Defines a max function and uses it to print the larger of fields 2 and 3 for each line.

sections.title: Multi-File Processing
sections.content: awk processes multiple files in sequence. FNR resets per file while NR continues. Use FILENAME to identify which file.
sections.example: awk 'FILENAME != prev {if(prev) print "---"; prev=FILENAME} {print}' file1.txt file2.txt
sections.explanation: Processes multiple files and adds a separator between them. FNR==1 could also detect file boundaries.

sections.title: String Functions
sections.content: awk has built-in string functions: length, substr, index, split, tolower, toupper, sub, gsub, sprintf.
sections.example: awk -F',' '{name=toupper($2); printf "%s works in %s\n", name, $3}' employees.csv
sections.explanation: toupper converts to uppercase. sub/gsub are sed-like substitutions within awk. sprintf returns formatted string.

common_mistakes: Using print instead of printf when formatting matters — printf gives control over alignment and precision
Forgetting that getline consumes a line — it advances the file pointer
Not using FNR vs NR correctly — NR is global, FNR resets per file
Using == for assignment instead of = — == is comparison, = is assignment
best_practices: Use BEGIN to print report headers and initialize variables
Use printf for all tabular output — it's always cleaner than print
Keep awk programs in separate .awk files for complex logic: awk -f program.awk
Use meaningful variable names even in one-liners — future you will thank you

exercises.prompt: Print a formatted table of employees with name (left-aligned, 20 chars), department, and salary (right-aligned, 8 chars)
exercises.hint: Use printf with %-20s for left-aligned name and %8.2f for salary

exercises.prompt: Calculate the total salary from employees.csv and print it with a formatted header
exercises.solution: awk -F',' 'BEGIN {print "=== Salary Report ==="} NR>1 {sum+=$4} END {printf "Total: $%.2f\n", sum}' employees.csv
exercises.hint: Use BEGIN for header, sum in main block, printf in END

quiz.question: What is the difference between NR and FNR?
options: NR is the total line count across all files, FNR resets per file
NR counts records, FNR counts fields
NR is for numbers, FNR is for strings
quiz.answer: NR is the total line count across all files, FNR resets per file
quiz.explanation: NR increments across all input files. FNR resets to 1 for each new file. Use FNR==1 to detect file boundaries.

quiz.question: To format output with specific column widths in awk, use function ___
quiz.explanation: printf gives C-style formatted output: %-20s for left-aligned strings, %8.2f for formatted floats, %05d for zero-padded integers.

lessons.title: File Comparison: join, diff & comm
lessons.introduction: Comparing and merging sorted files is a common task. join merges on a key field, diff shows line-by-line differences, and comm compares sorted lists. Together with paste and column, they form a complete file comparison toolkit.
lessons.purpose: Compare, merge, and combine sorted files using join, diff, comm, paste, and column
lessons.syntax: join FILE1 FILE2  |  diff FILE1 FILE2  |  comm FILE1 FILE2

sections.title: diff: Line-by-Line Comparison
sections.content: diff shows differences between two files. -u for unified format (most common), -y for side-by-side, -q for brief (just 'are different').
sections.example:
diff -u old_config.txt new_config.txt
diff -y server_old.log server_new.log | head -30
sections.explanation: Unified format shows context around changes (used in patches). Side-by-side is visual. -q just tells you if files differ.

sections.title: diff for Patches
sections.content: diff -u generates patches. Apply with patch. Reverse with patch -R. This is the foundation of how code patches work.
sections.example:
diff -u original.py modified.py > changes.patch
patch original.py < changes.patch
patch -R original.py < changes.patch  # undo
sections.explanation: Patches are portable text files that describe changes. Git diffs are essentially unified diffs.

sections.title: comm: Sorted List Comparison
sections.content: comm compares two sorted files column by column: lines only in file1, lines only in file2, lines in both. Must be pre-sorted.
sections.example:
sort old_list.txt > sorted_old.txt
sort new_list.txt > sorted_new.txt
comm sorted_old.txt sorted_new.txt
sections.explanation: Column 1 = only in old, column 2 = only in new, column 3 = in both. Use -1, -2, -3 to suppress columns.

sections.title: join: Merge on Key Field
sections.content: join merges two files on a common field (like SQL JOIN). Both files must be sorted on the join field. Default is field 1.
sections.example:
join -1 1 -2 1 employees.csv departments.csv
join -t',' -1 2 -2 1 employees.csv departments.csv
sections.explanation: -1 and -2 specify which field to join on in each file. -t sets the delimiter. Like an inner SQL JOIN.

sections.title: paste: Merge by Lines
sections.content: paste combines files side-by-side, line by line. -d sets the delimiter. Useful for merging columns from different sources.
sections.example:
paste -d',' names.txt salaries.txt > combined.csv
paste -s -d'+' numbers.txt | bc
sections.explanation: paste joins lines from multiple files. -s merges all lines of one file into one line. Useful for creating CSVs or computing sums.

sections.title: column: Format as Table
sections.content: column -t formats text into aligned columns. -s sets the delimiter. Great for making output human-readable.
sections.example:
awk -F',' '{print $2, $3, $4}' employees.csv | column -t
mount | column -t
sections.explanation: column -t auto-aligns columns based on the longest entry in each. Makes any whitespace or delimiter-separated data readable.

common_mistakes: Using comm on unsorted files — it requires pre-sorted input
Confusing diff -y (side-by-side) with diff -u (unified) — they serve different purposes
Not specifying field numbers with join — defaults to field 1 in both files
Using diff on binary files — it produces garbage; use cmp instead
best_practices: Always use diff -u for patches — it's the standard format
Sort files before using comm or join — they require sorted input
Use column -t to make any tabular output human-readable
Combine comm -23 to get 'only in file1' (lines unique to first file)

exercises.prompt: Compare two files and show only the lines that exist in the first file but not the second
exercises.hint: comm -23 suppresses columns 2 and 3, leaving only lines unique to file1

exercises.prompt: Format the employees.csv data as an aligned table with column headers
exercises.solution: head -1 employees.csv | tr ',' ' '; echo '---'; awk -F',' 'NR>1 {printf "%s %s %.2f\n", $2, $3, $4}' employees.csv | column -t
exercises.hint: Use column -t to auto-align, awk for formatting

quiz.question: What must you do before using comm to compare two files?
quiz.explanation: comm requires both input files to be sorted. It compares line by line assuming sorted order. Use sort or process substitution.

quiz.question: To merge two files side-by-side line by line, use command ___
quiz.explanation: paste combines corresponding lines from multiple files into single lines. Use -d to set the delimiter between columns.

lessons.title: Parallel Processing: xargs -P & GNU parallel
lessons.introduction: Modern systems have multiple CPU cores — but most Unix tools are single-threaded. xargs -P and GNU parallel let you run multiple processes concurrently, turning hours of sequential work into minutes of parallel execution.
lessons.purpose: Execute commands in parallel using xargs -P, GNU parallel, and process substitution
lessons.syntax: xargs -P N CMD  |  parallel [OPTIONS] CMD ::: ARGS  |  paste <(cmd1) <(cmd2)

sections.title: xargs -P: Parallel Execution
sections.content: xargs -P N runs up to N processes in parallel. Combine with -I{} for one-at-a-time processing. -n controls items per batch.
sections.example:
find . -name '*.gz' | xargs -P 4 -I{} gunzip {}
find . -name '*.log' | xargs -P $(nproc) -I{} grep -l ERROR {}
sections.explanation: -P 4 runs up to 4 gunzip processes simultaneously. $(nproc) uses all CPU cores.

sections.title: xargs Parallel Patterns
sections.content: Combine -P with -n (items per batch) and -I{} (placeholder) for flexible parallel execution.
sections.example:
cat urls.txt | xargs -P 8 -n 1 -I{} curl -sO {}
seq 1 100 | xargs -P 4 -I{} sh -c 'echo Processing {}'
sections.explanation: Downloads 8 URLs concurrently, one at a time per process. Processes numbers 1-100 with 4 workers.

sections.title: GNU parallel: The Power Tool
sections.content: GNU parallel is more powerful than xargs -P: handles arguments better, provides progress bar, and supports job slots.
sections.example:
parallel gzip ::: *.log
parallel -j 4 --progress gzip ::: *.log
parallel -j 2 curl -s {} ::: $(cat urls.txt)
sections.explanation: parallel -j 4 limits to 4 jobs. --progress shows a progress bar. ::: passes arguments directly.

sections.title: parallel with Input Files
sections.content: GNU parallel can read input from files, combine multiple inputs, and apply complex templates.
sections.example:
parallel echo {1} {2} ::: A B C ::: 1 2 3
parallel --colsep ',' echo {1} {2} < data.csv
sections.explanation: Combines multiple input sources. --colsep splits CSV columns into {1}, {2}, etc.

sections.title: Process Substitution for Parallelism
sections.content: Use <(cmd) to feed parallel consumers. Multiple process substitutions run commands concurrently.
sections.example:
diff <(sort file1.txt) <(sort file2.txt)
awk '{print $1}' <(cat a.log) | sort > merged.txt
sections.explanation: Process substitution runs commands in background and feeds their output as file arguments.

sections.title: Monitoring Parallel Jobs
sections.content: Track parallel job status with --joblog, --eta for time estimates, and --timeout for safety.
sections.example:
parallel --joblog /tmp/log.txt --eta --timeout 30 gzip ::: *.log
parallel --joblog /tmp/log.txt --progress --delay 0.1 wget -q {} ::: $(cat urls.txt)
sections.explanation: --joblog records completion status. --eta estimates remaining time. --timeout kills slow jobs.

common_mistakes: Running too many parallel jobs — can overwhelm disk I/O or network. Start with -P $(nproc)
Using xargs -P without -I{} — multiple items may be passed to one command invocation
Forgetting that parallel processes share stdout — output may be interleaved
Not using --timeout with parallel — hung jobs can block the pipeline indefinitely
best_practices: Start with -P 4 and increase if the system handles it well
Use GNU parallel for complex jobs — it handles edge cases better than xargs -P
Redirect parallel output to files to avoid interleaved terminal output
Use --joblog to track which jobs completed and which failed

exercises.prompt: Compress all .log files in the current directory using 4 parallel gzip processes
exercises.hint: Use find to list files, pipe to xargs -P 4 for parallel compression

exercises.prompt: Use GNU parallel to download 5 URLs concurrently with a progress bar
exercises.hint: Use parallel -j 5 for 5 concurrent jobs with --progress

quiz.question: What does xargs -P 4 do?
options: Runs up to 4 processes in parallel
quiz.answer: Runs up to 4 processes in parallel
quiz.explanation: -P N limits the number of concurrent processes to N. Combined with input, it processes items in parallel.

quiz.question: To limit GNU parallel to 3 concurrent jobs, use flag ___
quiz.explanation: parallel -j 3 runs at most 3 jobs simultaneously. Use -j $(nproc) for all CPU cores.

tracks.name: Data Analysis Pipeline
tracks.description: Parse, transform, aggregate, and report on structured data using command-line tools.

lessons.title: CSV Data Analysis
lessons.introduction: CSV files are everywhere — exports from databases, spreadsheets, and APIs. Learning to parse, transform, and analyze CSVs with awk, cut, sort, and other tools turns raw data into actionable insights without leaving the terminal.
lessons.purpose: Parse, transform, aggregate, and pivot CSV data using command-line tools

sections.title: CSV Parsing Fundamentals
sections.content: CSVs use commas as delimiters. Use awk -F',' or cut -d',' to split fields. Always skip headers with NR>1 or tail -n +2.
sections.example: awk -F',' 'NR>1 {print $2, $4}' employees.csv
sections.explanation: Extracts name and salary from each data row, skipping the header line.
