sections.title: Column Extraction and Transformation
sections.content: cut extracts specific columns. awk can reorder, combine, and transform fields. tr can change delimiters.
sections.example:
cut -d',' -f2,3 employees.csv | head -5
awk -F',' 'NR>1 {print $3, $2}' employees.csv | head -5
sections.explanation: cut extracts columns by number. awk can reorder columns (print $3, $2 swaps columns 2 and 3).

sections.title: Aggregation and Grouping
sections.content: Use awk with associative arrays to group and aggregate. Sort and count for frequency analysis.
sections.example: awk -F',' 'NR>1 {groups[$3]++; sum[$3]+=$4} END {for(g in groups) printf "%s: %d employees, avg salary $%.2f\n", g, groups[g], sum[g]/groups[g]}' employees.csv
sections.explanation: Groups by department (field 3), counts employees and sums salaries, then computes averages in the END block.

sections.title: Filtering and Sorting
sections.content: Filter rows with awk patterns. Sort by any column. Use head/tail for top/bottom N.
sections.example: awk -F',' 'NR>1 && $4>50000 {print}' employees.csv | sort -t',' -k4 -rn
sections.explanation: Filters employees with salary > 50000, then sorts by salary descending.

sections.title: CSV to Other Formats
sections.content: Convert CSV to TSV, JSON, or other formats using awk, sed, or tr. Handle edge cases like quoted fields.
sections.example: awk -F',' 'NR==1 {for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) printf "%s\t", $i; print ""} NR>1 {for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) printf "%s\t", $i; print ""}' employees.csv | column -t
sections.explanation: Converts CSV to tab-separated format and formats it as a table. Traverses all fields with a loop.

sections.title: Pivot-Style Analysis
sections.content: Create pivot-table-like summaries by grouping on one field and computing aggregates per group.
sections.example: awk -F',' 'NR>1 {key=$3; val[$3]+=$4; cnt[$3]++} END {for(k in val) printf "%s: sum=$%.0f avg=$%.0f count=%d\n", k, val[k], val[k]/cnt[k], cnt[k]}' employees.csv | sort
sections.explanation: Produces a department-level summary with sum, average, and count — like a SQL GROUP BY.

common_mistakes: Not handling CSVs with quoted fields containing commas — awk -F',' breaks on these
Using cut for CSVs with quoted fields — cut is purely delimiter-based, no quote awareness
Forgetting NR>1 — the header row gets mixed into numeric calculations
Not using -t',' with sort — default sort uses whitespace as delimiter
best_practices: For simple CSVs, awk is faster and more flexible than external tools
Always verify field positions with head -1 before writing complex pipelines
Use column -t to make output readable for quick inspection
For production CSV processing with quoted fields, consider csvtool or miller (mlr)

exercises.prompt: Calculate the average salary per department from employees.csv
exercises.solution: awk -F',' 'NR>1 {sum[$3]+=$4; cnt[$3]++} END {for(d in sum) printf "%s: $%.2f\n", d, sum[d]/cnt[d]}' employees.csv
exercises.hint: Group by department (field 3), sum salaries, divide by count in END block

exercises.prompt: List all unique departments from employees.csv, sorted alphabetically
exercises.hint: Extract field 3, deduplicate with sort -u

quiz.question: Why should you skip the first line of a CSV when doing numeric calculations?
options: The first line is always blank
The first line contains column headers, not data
The first line has wrong data types
awk can't process the first line
quiz.answer: The first line contains column headers, not data
quiz.explanation: CSV files typically have a header row with column names. Including it in numeric calculations would cause errors or incorrect results.

quiz.question: To count employees per department from a CSV, group on field 3 with awk's ___
quiz.explanation: awk's associative arrays (dept_count[$3]++) let you group and count by any field value — no pre-sorting needed.

lessons.title: Log Aggregation & Time-Series Analysis
lessons.introduction: Production systems generate massive logs. Aggregating logs from multiple sources, analyzing time-series patterns, and correlating events across files are critical skills for operations, security, and performance engineering.
lessons.purpose: Combine, aggregate, and analyze logs across multiple files and time ranges

sections.title: Multi-File Log Merging
sections.content: Combine logs from multiple files into a unified timeline. Sort by timestamp to merge chronologically.
sections.example: cat apache.log nginx.log | sort -k4 | tail -20
sections.explanation: Merges Apache and nginx logs and sorts by timestamp (field 4). Shows the 20 most recent events across both servers.

sections.title: Time-Windowed Analysis
sections.content: Extract events within a specific time range using awk timestamp comparison. Essential for incident investigation.
sections.example:
awk '$4~/\[14:0[0-9]:/ {print}' apache.log | wc -l
awk '$4~/\[09:[0-5][0-9]:/ {count[$7]++} END {for(url in count) print count[url], url}' apache.log | sort -rn | head -5
sections.explanation: First: count requests during the 14:00 hour. Second: top 5 URLs during 9:00-9:59 AM.

sections.title: Error Rate Calculation
sections.content: Calculate error rates as percentages over time windows. Compare error rates between periods.
sections.example: awk 'BEGIN{t=0;e=0} {t++; if($9>=500) e++} END {printf "Error rate: %.2f%% (%d/%d)\n", e/t*100, e, t}' apache.log
sections.explanation: Computes the overall 5xx error rate. Useful for monitoring dashboards and SLO tracking.

sections.title: Rate and Throughput Analysis
sections.content: Calculate requests per second, bytes per minute, or other throughput metrics from timestamped logs.
sections.example: awk -F'[: \[]' '{minute=$5":"$6; bytes[$minute]+=$10} END {for(m in bytes) printf "%s: %.2f MB\n", m, bytes[m]/1048576}' apache.log | sort
sections.explanation: Aggregates bandwidth per minute. Shows data transfer patterns over time.

sections.title: Anomaly Detection
sections.content: Find outliers in log patterns — IPs with unusual request counts, unusual status code distributions, or timing anomalies.
sections.example: awk '{count[$1]++} END {avg=0; n=0; for(ip in count){sum+=count[ip]; n++}; avg=sum/n; for(ip in count) if(count[ip]>avg*3) printf "ANOMALY: %s (%d requests, avg %.0f)\n", ip, count[ip], avg}' apache.log
sections.explanation: Finds IPs making more than 3x the average number of requests — potential bots or attacks.

sections.title: Log Report Generation
sections.content: Generate structured summary reports from raw logs. Combine multiple analyses into a single formatted output.
sections.example:
echo "=== Log Summary ==="
echo "Total requests: $(wc -l < apache.log)"
echo "Unique IPs: $(awk '{print $1}' apache.log | sort -u | wc -l)"
echo "Error rate: $(awk '{t++;if($9>=500)e++}END{printf "%.1f%%",e/t*100}' apache.log)"
echo "Top URL: $(awk '{print $7}' apache.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -1 | awk '{print $2}')"
sections.explanation: A complete log summary script combining multiple one-liners into a formatted report.

common_mistakes: Merging logs without sorting by timestamp — events appear out of order
Assuming all log formats are identical across services — field positions may differ
Not handling timezone differences when correlating logs from multiple servers
Using cat on compressed logs — use zcat/zgrep for .gz files
best_practices: Always sort by timestamp when merging multiple log sources
Use awk for most aggregations — it's faster than chaining sort|uniq|sort
Cache expensive computations: save intermediate results with tee
Use zcat/zgrep for compressed log files to avoid decompressing first

exercises.prompt: Count the number of requests per hour from apache.log
exercises.hint: Extract hour:minute from the timestamp field, then count occurrences

exercises.prompt: Find the top 3 most common error messages in server.log
exercises.solution: grep 'ERROR' server.log | awk -F'ERROR: ' '{print $2}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3
exercises.hint: Extract the message after ERROR:, then count and sort

quiz.question: When merging logs from multiple servers, what should you sort by first?
options: By timestamp to maintain chronological order
quiz.answer: By timestamp to maintain chronological order
quiz.explanation: When correlating events across servers, chronological order is essential. Sort by timestamp to see events in the order they actually occurred.

quiz.question: To search a compressed .gz log file without decompressing, use ___ instead of grep
quiz.explanation: zgrep (and zcat) work directly on gzipped files, decompressing on-the-fly. Much more efficient than decompressing to a temp file first.

lessons.title: Report Generation with awk & printf
lessons.introduction: Raw data is useless without presentation. Generating formatted reports — with headers, summaries, aligned columns, and visual elements — transforms data analysis into actionable documentation. awk's printf and formatting capabilities make this possible entirely from the command line.
lessons.purpose: Generate professional, formatted reports from raw data using awk and printf

sections.title: Report Headers and Footers
sections.content: Use BEGIN for headers, END for summaries and footers. Combine with separators for professional formatting.
sections.example: awk -F',' 'BEGIN {print "="; print "EMPLOYEE REPORT"; print "="; printf "%-20s %-15s %10s\n", "Name", "Dept", "Salary"; print "-"} NR>1 {printf "%-20s %-15s %10.2f\n", $2, $3, $4} END {print "="}' employees.csv
sections.explanation: Creates a complete report with header, separator, formatted data rows, and footer.

sections.title: printf Format Specifiers
sections.content: Master printf format specifiers: %s (string), %d (integer), %f (float), %e (scientific), %x (hex). Width and alignment with - and numbers.
sections.explanation: Demonstrates left-aligned strings (-30s), right-aligned integers (10d), floats (10.2f), and percentages.

sections.title: Summary Statistics
sections.content: Calculate and display aggregated statistics: counts, sums, averages, min/max, percentiles.
sections.explanation: Computes count, average, min, max, and spread in a single awk pass. Uses comma formatting with %,.

sections.title: Visual Elements
sections.content: Add visual elements to reports: separators, arrows, bar charts using characters like # and =.
sections.example: awk -F',' 'NR>1 {count[$3]++} END {max=0; for(d in count) if(count[d]>max) max=count[d]; for(d in count) {bar=""; for(i=0;i<count[d]*20/max;i++) bar=bar"#"; printf "%-12s [%-20s] %d\n", d, bar, count[d]}}' employees.csv | sort
sections.explanation: Creates a horizontal bar chart showing department sizes. Bars are proportional to the maximum value.

sections.title: Multi-Section Reports
sections.content: Combine multiple analyses into a single report with sections, each with its own header.
sections.example:
echo "========================================"
echo "         SYSTEM HEALTH REPORT"
echo "========================================"
echo ""
echo "--- Disk Usage ---"
df -h | head -5
echo ""
echo "--- Top Processes ---"
ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -6
echo ""
echo "--- Recent Errors ---"
grep -c ERROR server.log | xargs -I{} echo "Total errors: {}"
echo "========================================"
sections.explanation: Builds a multi-section report combining system metrics from different sources.

sections.title: Automated Report Scripts
sections.content: Package report generation into reusable scripts with parameters for date ranges, output formats, and destinations.
sections.explanation: A complete report script with date stamping, parameterized awk, and output to file.

common_mistakes: Using print instead of printf — print doesn't support formatting
Not aligning columns — inconsistent spacing looks unprofessional
Forgetting to handle division by zero in averages
Hardcoding report titles — use variables so scripts are reusable
best_practices: Always use printf for tabular output — it guarantees alignment
Include timestamps in reports for traceability
Use -v to pass shell variables into awk programs
Test report formatting with small data first, then scale up

exercises.prompt: Generate a formatted salary report from employees.csv showing name, department, salary, and a header/footer
exercises.solution: awk -F',' 'BEGIN {print "="; printf "%-20s %-15s %10s\n", "Name", "Department", "Salary"; print "-"} NR>1 {printf "%-20s %-15s $%9.2f\n", $2, $3, $4} END {print "="}' employees.csv
exercises.hint: Use BEGIN for header, printf for aligned columns, END for footer

exercises.prompt: Create a summary report showing total and average request size from apache.log
exercises.solution:
awk '{sum+=$10; cnt++} END {printf "Total requests: %d
Total bytes: %,d
Avg size: %,d bytes
", cnt, sum, sum/cnt}' apache.log
exercises.hint: Sum field 10 (bytes), count lines, compute average in END block

quiz.question: In awk's printf, what does %-20s do?
options: Right-aligns a string in a 20-character field
Left-aligns a string in a 20-character field
Prints a string truncated to 20 characters
quiz.answer: Left-aligns a string in a 20-character field
quiz.explanation: The - flag means left-align. 20 is the minimum width. So %-20s pads the string with spaces on the right to fill 20 characters.

quiz.question: To pass a shell variable into an awk program, use the -v flag: awk -v varname=___
quiz.explanation: awk -v varname=$value passes a shell variable into awk. Inside awk, reference it as varname (no $).

lessons.title: JSON & XML Processing: jq, xmllint & xmlstarlet
lessons.introduction: JSON and XML dominate modern data exchange. jq transforms JSON with a powerful filter language, while xmllint and xmlstarlet query and transform XML. These tools let you extract, filter, and reshape structured data entirely from the command line.
lessons.purpose: Query, filter, and transform JSON and XML data using command-line tools
lessons.syntax: jq 'FILTER' FILE  |  xmllint --xpath 'QUERY' FILE  |  xmlstarlet sel 'QUERY' FILE

sections.title: jq: JSON Fundamentals
sections.content: jq extracts and transforms JSON. .key accesses fields, .[] iterates arrays, | pipes to filters, select() filters elements.
sections.example:
cat data.json | jq '.users[] | {name: .name, email: .email}'
jq '.employees[] | select(.salary > 50000)' data.json
sections.explanation: Reshapes JSON output to show only name and email. select() filters to employees earning over 50k.

sections.title: jq Filters and Transformations
sections.content: jq supports map, sort_by, group_by, reduce, and string interpolation. Build complex transformations from simple building blocks.
sections.example:
jq 'map({name: .name, dept: .department})' data.json
jq 'sort_by(.salary) | reverse' data.json
jq 'group_by(.department) | map({dept: .[0].department, count: length})' data.json
sections.explanation: map transforms each element. sort_by orders by a field. group_by groups like SQL GROUP BY.

sections.title: jq: Combining with Shell
sections.content: Pass shell variables into jq with --arg. Output raw strings with -r. Construct JSON with {}.
sections.example:
NAME='Alice'
curl -s https://api.example.com/users | jq --arg name "$NAME" '.[] | select(.name == $name)'
jq -r '.[] | "\(.name): \(.email)"' data.json
sections.explanation: --arg passes shell variables. -r outputs raw strings. String interpolation with \() embeds expressions.

sections.title: xmllint: XML Querying
sections.content: xmllint queries XML with XPath expressions. --xpath selects nodes, --format prettifies, --dtd validates.
sections.example:
xmllint --xpath '//employee/name/text()' data.xml
xmllint --xpath '//employee[@dept="engineering"]' data.xml
xmllint --format data.xml
sections.explanation: XPath // selects all matching nodes. @attr matches attributes. text() extracts text content.

sections.title: xmlstarlet: XML Transformation
sections.content: xmlstarlet sel selects elements, ed edits, and tr transforms with XSLT. More powerful than xmllint for complex operations.
sections.example:
xmlstarlet sel -t -v '//employee/name' data.xml
xmlstarlet sel -t -m '//employee' -v 'name' -o ',' -v 'salary' -n data.xml
xmlstarlet ed -u '//employee[@id="1"]/salary' -v '75000' data.xml
sections.explanation: sel -t -v selects text values. -m iterates elements. -o outputs literal text. ed updates values.

sections.title: CSV to JSON Conversion
sections.content: Convert CSV to JSON using awk or jq for processing in JSON-native tools. Build JSON arrays from structured text.
sections.example:
awk -F',' 'NR>1 {printf "{\"name\":\"%s\",\"dept\":\"%s\",\"salary\":%s}\n", $2, $3, $4}' employees.csv | jq -s '.'
jq -R -s 'split("\n") | map(select(length>0) | split(",") | {name: .[0], dept: .[1], salary: .[2] | tonumber})' employees.csv
sections.explanation: Builds JSON objects from CSV fields. jq -s slurps all lines into an array for batch processing.

common_mistakes: Using jq without -r — output includes quotes around strings
Forgetting that xmllint --xpath requires well-formed XML — invalid XML fails silently
Confusing jq .key (accesses field) with .key[] (iterates) — context matters
Not using jq -s for slurping multiple JSON objects into an array
best_practices: Use jq -r for raw string output in shell scripts — no extra quotes
Build jq filters incrementally — test each pipe stage before adding the next
Use xmlstarlet sel for complex XPath queries — it handles more edge cases than xmllint
Validate XML before processing with xmllint --noout to catch structural errors

exercises.prompt: Using jq, extract all names and salaries from employees.json where salary exceeds 50000
exercises.hint: Use jq select() to filter and {} to reshape the output

exercises.prompt: Convert employees.csv to a JSON array using awk and jq
exercises.hint: Use awk to build JSON objects and jq -s to slurp into an array

quiz.question: What does jq -r do differently from plain jq?
options: Runs jq in raw mode without any output
Outputs strings without surrounding double quotes

quiz.question: To iterate over all elements in a JSON array with jq, use filter ___
quiz.explanation: .[] iterates over all elements in an array. Combine with select(), map(), and other filters for powerful transformations.
